Biographies   
 
 
Research Organisations and Digital Experts  
 
The AIDCC will leverage ARM Hub’s 13 core staff, 47 experts (including leading university 
researchers), Board members, and Advisors, are Australia’s leaders in the design and delivery of 
technology adoption and R&D commercialisation outcomes for SMEs.  
A full list of biographies of the ARM Hub team is listed below. Most recently ARM Hub CEO, 
Associate Professor Cori Stewart, was awarded the prestigious Women in AI Awards Australia and 
New Zealand for 2022  for AI in Manufacturing .  
The AIDCC’s executive team  has decades of leadership experience in industry and innovation policy, 
university R&D commercialisation, and technical and management fields in AI, robotics, engineering, 
design, innovation, entrepreneurship, IP commercialisation, communications, project  management, 
and high -calibre science and technology facility operations, necessary to successfully deliver and 
grow the AIDCC.  
It is precisely the above track record and capabilities that ensures the successful delivery of the 
AIDCC and its contribution to a sustainable long -term Australian infrastructure supporting SMEs to 
scale and create Australia’s sovereign industrial capability and access to high -value global markets.   
The ARM Hub team is supported by a strong Board, who along with the CEO, have bee n instrumental 
in establishing the policy arguments and evidence that has inspired the development of the AIDCC 
program itself. The Chair of the ARM Hub Board is Emeritus Professor Roy Green, Innovation 
Advisor, University of Technology Sydney. Professor G reen holds numerous prestigious national and 
international government, business and university appointments and is a figurehead for Australia’s 
industrial digital transformation agenda and the reinvigoration of the country’s innovation 
ecosystem.   
The AIDC C has six investing Queensland university partners, represented by 47 researchers who 
contribute to projects and industry engagement activities, including working as part of a National 
Network, as detailed in the Project Plan, and support from CSIRO’s Data 61.   
 
QUEENSLAND UNIVERSITY OF TECHNOLOGY  (QUT)  
  
QUT is a major contributor to the AIDCC through the Centre for Robotics,  Centre for Data Science, 
Centre for Future Enterprise, and Design School.    
  
QUT Centre for Robotics   
 
The Centre builds on a decade of investment in world -leading robotics research and translation, 
funded through programs including the Australian Resear ch Council’s Centre of Excellence in Robotic 
Vision, Cooperative Research Centres, industry and QUT initiatives. The Centre is led by 
Distinguished Professor Peter Corke and Professor Michael Milford who are both contributors to the 
AIDCC.

Biographies   
 
 
The Centre for  Robotics is at the forefront of research and innovation in AI -enabled robotics, 
including computer vision, localisation and mapping, digital twins, machine learning and planning.  
 
The Centre translates research into commercial and societal outcomes, e.g., in mining, defence, 
precision agriculture, autonomous vehicles, manufacturing and healthcare applications; leads 
education, training and development of talent to meet growing deman ds; and provides leadership in 
technological policy development and societal debate, e.g., drone shared airspace, trusted systems 
and eXplainable AI.  
 
Key domains of AI expertise  
• Physical interaction  – explores how the physical world can be translated to  the digital.  
Beyond cyber -physical system interaction, researchers are embodying AI in robotic systems, 
sensing important real -world data, and advancing force -mediated control methods.  
• Perception and localisation  – utilises advanced computational vision,  feature selection and 
neuroscience -inspired AI, such as RatSLAM, to create maps, and calculates and tracks its 
location in the world.  
• Visual learning and understanding  – investigates how AI perception can be made safe, 
trustworthy, and reliable, e.g. for  people detection in hazardous workplaces.  Understanding 
is developed through object -based semantic maps, graphs, and symbolic rule mining.  
• Decision and control  – investigates how AI can make autonomous decisions and control for 
robots in the presence of  uncertainty, e.g., probabilistic (Bayesian) reasoning. Advanced data 
analysis detects anomalous conditions in weak measurement environments, such as invasive 
species detection in agriculture and on reefs.   
• Human interaction  – how AI can effectively inter act with humans, including how humans 
interact, perceive and trust AI, especially concurrent symbolic and post -hoc deep -learning 
techniques in eXplainable AI.  
  
 QUT Centre for Data Science   
  
The Centre draws together capability in data science from acros s Australia and is a global leader of 
frontier methods for the use of data. Led by Distinguished Professor Kerrie Mengersen, the Centre’s 
work supports R esponsible AI, including ethical, governance, sovereign, also data management and 
data literacy.   
The Centre builds the tools to deliver Responsible AI, using analytical methods, visualisation and 
aggregating data sets using federated systems to maintain ownership/privacy. Through federated 
analysis on data, the Centre identifies how to do ‘transfer learni ng’ from one system to another.  
The Centre uses different types of data, such as analysing emerging data forms such as video, natural 
language processing, virtual reality, satellite data and social media. The Centre also works with little 
data sets, as well as large, which is critical for emerging areas like biosecurity.  
 
The Centre will provide the AIDCC with a one -stop -shop to:

Biographies   
 
 
• Access Australia’s data science network and research capability   
• Bridge the gap between deep research and applications   
• Create a trusted source for advice on AI and data science issues  
• Bring together a critical mass of data science researchers to develop, and contribute to, 
state -of-the-art solutions (including NAIC and AIDCC’s collaboration on the ethical acc ess to 
large, shared data sets)   
• Create partnerships through an Australian data science network   
• Provide research and professional training opportunities to SMEs   
• Leverage investment in data science (e.g. strategic appointments, access to research 
infrastr ucture and relevant data assets, Australian Research Council Centres of Excellence 
and in eResearch).  
 
 
Key domains of AI expertise include:  
 
• Applied data science  – multi -faceted datasets obtained from big data sources are curated 
prior to deep learning an d natural language processing techniques for bespoke customer 
applications.  
• Data -focused decision making  – novel methods for Counterfactual Assumptions and 
removal of Representation Bias improve AI in visualisation, communication and 
interpretation of data . These analyses allow for improved decision -making, and the critical 
evaluation of issues related to the role and use of data science in society.  
• Models and algorithms – use of novel models, such as Sentiment Analysis, Graph Mining 
and extraction of Predi cate Rules from Deep Learning to describe and make decisions about 
complex real -world systems, and methods to ensure high quality, open, reproducible data 
science. The Centre develops scalable, efficient computational algorithms for analysing 
dimensional a nd highly structure data.  
• Data for discovery  – advancing the medical, physical, technological and social sciences 
through the development and application of new data science methods in non-parametric 
and distribution free  models to achieve rigorous scienti fic discovery and generate evidence -
based insights.  
 
 QUT Centre for Future Enterprise (CFE)   
  
The CFE includes world -renowned strategy, technology, and innovation management experts that 
will work with the AIDCC to support SMEs and microenterprises, acro ss regional and urban areas, in 
the areas of AI Governance, AI Business Models and Applications of AI. CFE will contribute PhD 
students to projects aligned to topic areas and in relevant programs, such as the AI Industry Fellows 
initiative and the AI Suppl y Chain Innovation program activities.    
  
 QUT School of Design   
  
The School leads applied research on how to design robots that work better with humans. The 
School contributes to the AIDCC by engaging with industry to build toolkits for the rapid prototyping 
of collaborative robotics solutions, and leveraging multimodal interaction, including Augmented

Reality and Virtual Reality, with robotics systems. These teams will collaborate with selected industry 
partners including Australian Expedition Veh icles, which makes Australian Defence Force and 
International Defence Industry military vehicles and is 100% Indigenous -owned, Veteran company, 
located in Townsville Queensland.    
 
JAMES COOK UNIVERSITY  
 
James Cook University (JCU) builds and applies AI tools in key areas of applied research. JCU has 
internationally -recognised research strengths in the Internet of Things (IoT) and is supported by 
innovative sensor technologies and engineering capability.  
JCU has built long -term industry partnerships across the country and specifically in North 
Queensland, which is the location of large -scale investments in hydrogen, critical minerals, clean 
energy, recycling, and other high -value resource industries – all urgently requiring access to the 
high -value skills that the AIDCC will offer.   
The AIDCC will have a second facility in JCU’s Townsville campus, with business and technical 
expertise and demonstration capabilities. Key programs such as the defence technolo gy accelerator 
(SPRINTS) program will be delivered in Townsville, alongside a corporate education Datathon 
focused on SME defence industry outcomes.  
JCU has committed its eResearch Centre and the Engineering Facility expertise to the AIDCC whose 
work is c haracterised by applying novel, collaborative, multidisciplinary and data/compute intensive 
applied research.    
 
UNIVERSITY OF QUEENSLAND (UQ) 
 
The strengths of contributing UQ experts span several areas of AI, machine learning, data science, 
computer visi on, data mining, human -centered AI, optimisation and statistics.  
Key manufacturing priority industries include medical, resources, defence, and clean energy as well 
as the critical cross -cutting field of cyber security. UQ also work extensively in agricul ture supporting 
digital SMEs to access global markets with leading AI and quantum computing capabilities.     
The UQ AI Collaboratory and the UQ Centre for Cyber Security are the key contributors to the AIDCC 
program, working on industry projects and engage ment activities. UQ also offers training to industry 
through dedicated Cyber Security SME short courses as well as AI short courses, including the 7 
Week introductory platform to AI 'Practical Deep Learning for Coders’ by Honorary UQ Professor 
Jeremy Howar d, Founder of fast.ai.    
UNIVERSITY OF SOUTHERN QUEENSLAND (USQ)  
  
USQ’s Centre for Agricultural Engineering (CEA) will be the partner for this AIDCC. Operating since 1994 its 
purpose is to develop solutions for a sustainable and profitable rural sector. Based in Toowoomba, the 
Centre delivers applied, practical and profitable solutions that strengthen productivity, energy use, 
bioresource recycling, sensing, AI, automation and robotics. CEA will work with selected AIDCC companies 
including Indyn P ty Ltd to build a bio secure AI platform for the grain industry .

GRIFFITH UNIVERSITY  
 
Griffith University, through its School for Exercise Science, is collaborating with the AIDCC on developing 
personalised digital twins for humans and implanted and wear able devices. These personalised digital 
twins are biophysics -based multiscale models of the human neuro -muscular -skeletal systems that are in 
part created and executed using AI. Griffith will be collaborating specifically with the AIDCC’s industry 
partner , VALD Performance, which provides high performance sport and tactical professionals the right 
information, for the right decision, at the right time.   
 
CENTRAL QUEENSLAND UNIVERSITY  
 
 CQU’s applied research strength in robotics, or mechatronic engineering, in its Mackay campus is the focus 
of the AIDCC collaboration.   CQU expertise includes inspection robots for condition assessment of 
infrastructure such as water pipes, and drones for commercial application highlighted in its collaboration 
with  Swarm Farm Robotics that delivers lightweight agricultural robots for farm operators to a global 
marketplace.   
 
CSIRO DATA61  
 
CSIRO’s Data61 is the data and digital specialist arm of Australia’s national science agency. Our vision is to 
be among the world's top five in trusted and responsible AI science and technology, making Australia’s 
adoption of mathematically rigorous AI safe, secure, and reliable. Through our Responsible AI and our 
Foundational Machine Learning programs, there are clear goals to  enable SME adoption by making 
embedding rigorous trustworthy AI technologies as their competitive advantage and embed responsible AI 
into broader scientific discovery and technology development processes.  
 
 
EXPERTS  
  
 Distinguished Professor Peter Corke – Professor in Robotic Vision, Faculty of 
Engineering , QUT ; Member, ARM Hub Research Advisory Committee  
Peter Corke is a robotics researcher and educator with over 30 years’ 
experience in robotics theory and practice. He is the distinguished professo r of 
robotic vision at Queensland University of Technology, director of the QUT 
Centre for Robotics, and director of the ARC Centre of Excellence for Robotic 
Vision. His research is concerned with enabling robots to see, and the 
application of robots to mi ning, agriculture and environmental monitoring. He 
wrote the bestselling textbook “Robotics, Vision, and Control” and the Robot 
Academy online teaching resource.

Biographies   
 
 
 Distinguished Professor Kerrie Mengersen FAA FASSA – Australian Laureate  
Fellow, Faculty of Science , QUT  
Kerrie Mengersen is a Distinguished Research Professor in Statistical Science 
and the Director of the QUT Centre for Data Science at QUT and holds a 
concurrent role as Associate Member in the Department of Statistics at the 
University of Oxford, UK. She was a Deputy Director in the ARC Centre of 
Excellence in Mathematical and Statistical Frontiers (2015 -2021) and an ARC 
Laureate Fellow (2015 -2021). In 20 18 she was elected as a Fellow of the 
Australian Academy of Science (AAS), the  Academy of Social Sciences in 
Australia (ASSA) and the Queensland Academy of Arts and Sciences (QAAS). She 
is an active member of the Institute for Mathematical Sciences, Intern ational 
Biometrics Society, International Statistical Institute and the Statistical Society 
of Australia.  Professor Mengersen’s research focuses on using and developing 
new statistical and computational methods that can help to solve complex 
problems in t he real world. These problems are in the fields of environment, 
genetics, health and medicine, and industry. Her research interests include, 
complex systems modelling and Bayesian statistical modelling, computational 
methods and applications.  
 
 
 
 
 Professor Jonathan Roberts, ARM Hub Technical Director, Professor in 
Robotics, Faculty of Engineering, QUT ; Centre Director – Australian Cobotics 
Centre  
Jonathan Roberts is Professor in Robotics at Queensland University of 
Technology (QUT). His main resear ch interests are in the areas of Field Robotics, 
Design Robotics and Medical Robotics. He was a co -inventor of the UAV 
Challenge, an international flying robot competition. Before joining QUT, 
Professor Roberts was the Research Director of CSIRO’s Autonomo us Systems 
Laboratory where he developed projects in the area of museum robotics and 
telepresence. Professor Roberts is a Past President of the Australian Robotics & 
Automation Association, was a member of the Founding Editorial Board of the 
IEEE Journal o f Robotics and Automation Letters and currently serves as a 
Senior Editor.   He is the Centre Director of the Australian Cobotics Centre  which 
was established in August 2021  with a focus on the implementation of 
Collaborative Robotics (or Cobotics) within Australian manufacturing .

 Professor Will Browne, Professor and Chair in Manufacturing Robotics - 
Faculty of Engineering, QUT and ARM Hub  
Will Browne is Professor and Chair in Manufacturing Robotics at Queensland 
University of Technology (QUT) with ARM Hub and CSIRO. Possessing expe rtise 
in artificial cognitive systems, with interest in how systems, such as robots, can 
interact with the real -world to solve problems of interest. His topics of interest 
include computer vision and perception, explainable Artificial Intelligence (AI), 
transfer learning and collaborative robotics. Professor Browne’s 
interdisciplinary background in Mechanical Engineering, Energy Studies, 
Control, Cybernetics, Computer Science, Computational Neuroscience as well as 
AI and Robotics, is further expanding the d isciplines of the ARM Hub expert 
team.  
 
 
 
 Professor Michael Milford, Co -Director of the QUT Centre for Robotics 
Professor in Robotics, Faculty of Engineering ,  
Michael Milford conducts  interdisciplinary research at the boundary between 
robotics, neuroscience and computer vision and is a multi -award -winning 
educational entrepreneur. His research models the neural mechanisms in the 
brain underlying tasks like navigation and perception to develop new 
technologies in challenging application domains such as all -weather, anytime 
positioning for autonomous vehicles. He is also passionate about engaging and 
educating all sectors of society around new opportunities and impacts from 
technology inc luding robotics, autonomous vehicles and artificial intelligence.   
Professor Milford was named the top robotics researcher in Australia by citation 
impact by The Australian Research Magazine (2019) and was a top 3 finalist for 
the Australian Museum Eureka  Prize for Outstanding Early Career Researcher 
(2016), the  APEC ASPIRE Prize Finalist (2018) and was a finalist in the  Reimagine 
Education Awards Finalist K12 Category.  
 
 Professor Richi Nayak, Faculty of Science , QUT  
Richi Nayak is the Applied Data Science Program Leader of the University Centre 
for Data Science (CDS) and is an internationally recognised expert in data 
mining, text mining and web intelligence. She has combined knowledge in these 
areas very successfully  with diverse disciplines such as Social Science, Science, 
and Engineering for technology transfer to real -world problems to change their 
practices and methodologies.  Her research interests are machine learning and, 
in recent years, she has concentrated h er work on text mining, personalisation, 
automation, and social network analysis.  She has published high -quality 
conference and journal articles and is highly cited in her research field.  
Professor Nayak has received several awards and nominations for te aching, 
research and service activities.

 Professor David Lovell, Faculty of Science , QUT  
David Lovell is a Professor in the  QUT’s School of Computer Science , Deputy 
Director of  QUT’s Centre for Data Science , and leader of the Centre’s Data -
Focused Decisi on-Making Program.  He joined QUT in 2014 as Head of the 
School of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS).  Before joining 
QUT, he held numerous research management positions in CSIRO.  Professor 
Lovell was involved in a wide range of research and consulting in the analysis of 
large and complex datasets and was appointed Director of the Australian 
Bioinformatics Network and has been instrumental in the formation of ABACBS 
(Australian Bioinformatics and Computational Biology Society).  His resear ch 
interests lie at the intersection of humanity, science and technology, particularly 
data science.  
 
 Professor Marek Kowalkiewicz – Faculty of Business and Law , QUT  
Marek Kowalkiewicz  is an academic and industry leader with extensive 
experience in conducting research, co -innovating with industry and university 
partners, and delivering innovative products to the market. As founding director 
of Centre for the Digital Economy, he leads QU T’s research agenda to inform 
and influence a robust digital economy in Australia. Professor Kowalkiewicz 
manages a contemporary research portfolio and converts industry driven 
opportunities into research outcomes of global relevance. He is an invited 
gove rnment expert, university lecturer and project lead, as well as an inventor 
and author. He is recognised as a top -quality manager and excellent public 
speaker and has an interest in working with stakeholders in developing 
innovative ideas, ground -breaking business applications and high -impact new 
technologies.  
 Associate Professor Glenda Amayo Caldwell – Academic Lead Research, 
Faculty of Engineering , QUT  
Glenda Amayo Caldwell is a Senior Lecturer in Architecture, School of Design, 
Creative Industries Faculty at the Queensland University of Technology (QUT).  
She is a chief investigator in the IMCRC Design Robotics for Mass Customisation 
Manufacturing project in collaboration with UAP and RMIT. Embracing trans -
disciplinary approaches from arc hitecture and human computer interaction, her 
research places design at the forefront of robotic research for design -led and 
mass customization manufacturing. She is an active researcher in the QUT 
Design Lab and is the author of numerous publications in t he areas of media 
architecture, urban informatics, and design robotics.

 Associate Professor Jared Donovan – Academic Lead Research, Faculty of 
Creative Industries, Education & Social Justice , QUT  
Jared Donovan is a Senior Lecturer in Interaction Design at the Queensland 
University of Technology. He currently leads the ‘Design Robotics for Mass 
Customised Manufacturing’ research project with industry partner UAP (funded 
by IMCRC), which is developing new ways to use robots and vision sy stems for 
design led manufacturing. His main research interest is in how technologies can 
be made more useful and easier to use for people and how end -users can be 
involved in the design process to make technologies better.  
 
 Dr Muge Belek Fialho Teixeri a – Senior Lecturer, Faculty of Engineering , QUT  
Muge Belek Fialho Teixeira is an award -winning creative maker and 
transdisciplinary designer, who specialises in advanced manufacturing, digital 
fabrication, and parametric design. She is one of the chief in vestigators of QUT's 
Design Robotics project. In her career, she has worked with prominent 
architectural firms such as Zaha Hadid Architects, taught in several institutions 
including AA Visiting Schools, published articles, given interviews, and 
presented in many international conferences and exhibitions.  
 
 
 Associate Professor Markus Rittenbruch – Associate Professor in Interaction 
Design, Faculty of Creative Industries, Education & Social Justice , QUT  
Markus Rittenbruch is an Associate Professor in Int eraction Design at 
Queensland University of Technology (QUT). He is the Associate Director of the 
QUT Design Lab which hosts innovative research at the interplay of Design and 
Technology, such as the Design Robotics project. Professor Rittenbruch is an 
experienced researcher with over 20 years of experience in the design of 
human -centred technology. His work focuses on the design and study of 
emerging technologies, including collaborative systems, human -robot 
collaboration, social robotics, and extended rea lity. 
 
 Professor Greg Hearn – QUT and Chair, ARM Hub Strategic Research 
Committee  
Greg Hearn is Director of Commercial R&D in the Creative Industries Faculty at 
QUT and a research leader in the ARM Hub and QUT Design Lab. His research 
focuses on strategic industry futures, knowledge policy, and the future of work. 
He is author of over 2 0 major books and reports, most recently as editor of The 
Future of Creative Work: Creativity and Digital Disruption  (Edward Elgar, 2020). 
This book examines the impact of digital disruption, robotics, and AI, on jobs in 
design, art and media, and the crea tion of high value products and services 
across all sectors of the economy. He has worked in large R&D projects with 
private industry and public sector organisations over three decades, across 
many sectors including, aviation, defence, agriculture, and man ufacturing.

 Dr Chris Lehnert, Faculty of Engineering , QUT  
Chris Lehnert is a Senior Lecturer  within the Robotics and Autonomous Systems 
(RAS) group at QUT. His research interests lie in the development of novel 
methods for robotic manipulation in real world and challenging environments. A 
particular focus of his research is enabling robots to per form autonomous 
harvesting operations in horticulture. He was part of the Australian Centre for 
Robotics Vision team competing in the 2017 Amazon Robotics Challenge, where 
he led the development of the grasping and planning algorithms which could 
successfu lly grasp a large variety of objects in a cluttered environment. He is 
part of the Future Food Systems Co -operative Research Centre and will receive 
$35 million in funding over 10 years from the Federal Government, along with 
almost $150 million in support  from the research centre’s educational and 
commercial participants. He will be working on developing robotics and smart 
technology for vertical and indoor protected cropping.  
 
 Dr Rui Torres de Oliveira – Business Growth, Strategy and Innovation , QUT  
Rui Torres de Oliveira  is an academic at QUT Business School where he is an 
expert on innovation, strategy and International Business on the Australian 
Centre for Entrepreneurship - a world -leading hub in the field. Before joining 
QUT, he worked at the Unive rsity of Queensland and prior to that, he was a 
senior executive and worked in the US, China, and Europe. Dr Torres de Oliveira  
holds a Doctorate of Business Administration from Manchester Business School, 
an MBA and a Masters in Civil Engineering. He is p assionate about helping start -
ups and SMEs to drive innovation and bring their products or services to the 
market in the best possible conditions.  
 
 Professor Felipe Gonzalez – Faculty of Engineering , QUT  
Felipe Gonzalez is within the School of Electrical Engineering and Robotics (EER) 
and a CI in QUT Centre for Robotics (QCR) Engineering Faculty. He has a passion 
for innovation in the fields of aerial robotics and automation, and a particular 
interest in creating aerial robots, drones or UAVs th at possess a high level of 
cognition using efficient on -board computer algorithms using advanced 
optimisation and game theory approaches to assist us in understanding and 
improving our physical and natural world. He leads the Airborne Sensing Lab at 
QUT, a nd is co -author of several books in UAV -based remote sensing and design 
based on evolutionary optimization and game strategies. He is also a Chartered 
Professional Engineer, Engineers Australia – National Professional Engineers 
Register (NPER), a Member Ro yal Aeronautical Society (RAeS), The IEEE, 
American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AIAA) and Holder of a 
current Australian Private Pilot Licence (CASA PPL) and a Remote Pilot Licence 
(RePL from CASA).

 Dr Tim Williams – Industrial Design Lead , QUT  
Tim William’s career has been divided between design practice and academia 
giving him ideal perspective on the benefits of industry -university collaboration. 
Consequently, he has a strong track record of leading collaborative pr ojects with 
industry partners both locally and internationally. His background is Industrial 
Design with expertise in Computer Aided Design, Design for Manufacture, and 
Design for Electronics. Mr Williams is an authority on Product Ecosystem theory 
and has  diverse research interests including Design -Led innovation, 3D printing, 
transportation design and boat building.  
 
 
 Associate Professor Alice Payne, Circular Economy and  Textiles , School of 
Design , QUT   
Alice Payne is an Associate Professor in Fashion in the School of Design, a 
program leader in  Centre for a Waste -Free World , and co -leader of the research 
group  TextileR: Future Textile Industries .  Her research centres on 
environmental and social sustainability concerns throughout textile and apparel 
industry supply chains. Dr Payne has examined perspectives on sustainab ility 
along the cotton value chain, the cultural and material flows of post -consumer 
textile waste, and design processes of mass -market product developers, 
independent fashion designers, and social entrepreneurs. She is author of the 
book  Designing Fashion's Future: Present Practice and Tactics for Sustainable 
Change  (Bloomsbury 2021), co -author of  Fashion Trends: Analysis and 
Forecasting  (second edition, 2021) and co -editor of  Global Perspectives on 
Sustainable Fashion  (Bloomsbury 2019).  She is an award -winning designer an d 
has exhibited in Australia and overseas. In 2014 and 2020 her design work was 
featured in  A Practical Guide to Sustainable Fashion . Her recent work explores 
speculative approaches to textile design including design for disassembly and 
biotextiles.  
  
 Associate Professor Rafael Gomez – Design Lead , QUT  
Rafael Gomez is Study Area Coordinator for Industrial Design. He is a design 
researcher for QUT Design Lab and a prominent researcher in the field of 
emotional experience, wearable tech for medical/healt h applications and 
emerging technologies. He works closely with global industry partners and leads 
the BMW Group + QUT Design Academy which focuses on fostering design 
excellence, exploring new knowledge horizons and advancing cutting -edge 
technologies thr ough internships, research and special R+D projects with BMW 
Group in Germany.  Rafael has been a Council Member of the Design Institute of 
Australia Queensland Chapter, Founder and Chair of the Design and Emotion 
Society Australia Chapter and Committee Me mber for the 2015 IASDR 
International Design Conference.

 Associate Professor Ajay Pandey , Sensors and Intelligent Systems , QUT  
Ajay Pandey is Associate Professor at Queensland University of Technology 
(QUT) with expertise in bespoke sensor design and development of intelligent 
systems. His topics of interest include design and development of intelligent 
sensing and energy harvesting platform technologies with capabilities of on -
sensor and near -sensor computing. His research is centred on how autono mous 
systems such as robots can gain situational awareness akin to intelligent 
biological systems. He leads several interdisciplinarity projects on development 
of advanced vision, tactile and acoustic sensing technologies for medical 
robotics, infrastructu re monitoring, and sustainable engineering. Dr Pandey’s 
interdisciplinary background in Physics, Electrical Engineering, Materials Science 
and Energy Systems further expands ARM Hub’s advanced manufacturing 
capability in new domains of medical devices, mic ro/nano robotics and 
wearable electronics.  
 
 Mr Dan Christie, Head of Engineering , James Cook University (JCU)  
Mr Christie is currently the Head of Engineering at James Cook University.   At 
the time of receiving this award he was the Glencore Copper Refinery and Port 
Operations Manager in Townsville.  After graduating from James Cook 
University, with a Bachelor of Engineering with Honours in 1998,  Mr Christie 
obtained a Master of Science degree in Systems Engineering from 
Loughborough Universit y, UK.   Since 2010, he has been serving as a Manager 
and Superintendent at Glencore, a leading global natural resource company. Mr 
Christie has more than 15 years’ experience in various large -scale engineering 
projects, ranging from defence projects with t he Royal Australian Air Force to 
international resource projects with leading global mining and resource 
companies.   
 
 
 Professor Ian Atkinson, Professor and Director eResearch Centre , JCU  
Ian Atkinson  is a Tropical Leader and Director of the eResearch Centre at James 
Cook University. His PhD studies were in chemical physics but he moved from 
experimental science into computational chemistry and high -performance 
computing two decades.  Over the past dec ade, the rapid expansion of the 
Internet, mass data storage, and computing has impacted every area of research 
and academic activity. As Director of the JCU eResearch Centre he has the 
privilege of working with researchers to apply new and ever -changing IC T tools 
and methods to their research and amplifying their impacts.  Professor Atkinson 
has a long -standing interest in eResearch methods, tools, scientific data 
management and user interfaces for HPC tools. He is also actively involved in 
researching how new systems and software that connect the physical and 
virtual worlds, particularly focusing on environmental monitoring with sensor 
networks.

 Professor Nico Adams, Optus Chair of Digital Innovation (IoT), JCU 
Prior to joining JCU in December 2021, Ni co Adams was a n Associate Professor 
and Director of the Factory  of the Future at Swinburne University of Technology.  
He held the position of Senior  Research Scientist and Product Manager at 
CSIRO’s Data61  for over three years . Following on from his work w ith CSIRO and 
Data61, Dr Adams assumed the role of Program Lead for Digital Transformation 
and Industry 4.0 at the Innovative Manufacturing Cooperative Research Centre 
(IMCRC).  At IMCRC, he co -developed an innovation diagnostic and an Industry 
4.0 busines s, product and strategy framework tailored for small -to-medium 
sized businesses. Dr Adams is  also a Chief  Investigator at the Australian Cobotics 
Centre.  
  
 Dr Mostafa Rahimi Azghadi, Senior Lecturer, Electrical and Electronic 
Engineering , JCU  
Mostafa Rahimi is a recognised national and international scientist and 
leader, who was ranked in the top 2% of the highly cited EEE researchers 
in 2020. He is currently the Chair of the IEEE Northern Australia Section 
and the program coordinator for the J CU Electrical and Electronic 
Engineering degree. Dr Rahimi is the AI leader of the $5M ARC -funded

AIDCC National  Security Risk Assessment 
Plan 
There are three primary risks to be concerned about when considering the role of the ARM Hub in 
relation to national security, as outlined below.  
Export Controls  
Risk 
Export controls restrict  the transfer of materiel or information in controlled categories to foreign 
entities . There are several treaties and policies that define these categories  in Australia, which 
include conventional arms, nuclear material, and chemical or biological weapons and their 
precursors. Foreign entities can be defined as companies in foreign nation states or foreign persons 
living within Australia. There may be differing restrictions for different foreign entities. E xceptions to 
these restrictions can  only  be granted  by the Australian Government . 
In the case of international collaboration, other governments may impose their own export 
regulations (such as the ITAR regulations in the United States) on any projects that operate across borders, and these may surpass the restrictions under Australian law.  
Violating these controls deliberately or otherwise can have extremely severe consequences for companies and individuals.  
Considerations  
• Extremely severe legal and financial consequences  for violations of export controls  
• Cost of isolating project teams from others  
• Cost of implementing export controls office  
• Delays in communications caused by checks  
Mitigation  
The first mitigation is to limit dealings with foreign individuals to an absolute minimum on projects 
that require s uch precautions . Where practical, teams assigned to these projects should be isolated 
physically and digitally from others. This minimises the potential for any leaks through other 
mitigations .  
Secondly, an export controls office should be established to check all outgoing communications from 
teams  handling sensitive material and perform regular audits of all communications . This office can 
also maintain  training programs to educate individuals about the risks and responsibilities involved 
in working with sensitive material.  
Foreign Interference 
Risk 
Foreign interference refers to decisions and actions undertaken on behalf  of a foreign entity that are 
contrary to A ustralian interests.  The types of  actions  considered interference  and the responsibilities 
of organisations  to mitigate them  are specified  under Australian law . The potential  scope of these 
actions is quite broad  and can range from influencing staff opinio ns on strategy due to foreign 
funding opportunities  to doing  business with any  individuals or companies listed on DFAT’s 
Consolidated List of financially sanctioned entities.  There can be significant legal and practical consequences to organisations that s uccumb to foreign 
interference, although the specifics  may be unique in each case , but by definition, Australia’s 
interests are harmed in the process .  
Considerations  
• Practicality of exhaustive monitoring and policing  
• Necessity of exposure to foreign businesses and organisations  
• Cost of vetting foreign research and business partners  
• Wide ranging consequences for the organisation and Australia 
• Reliability of individual training and opportunity selection policies  
Mitigations 
For a research and collaboration focused organisation, there is little chance of eliminating 
interactions with foreign entities , and the  chance of any organisation  exhaustively monitoring all 
communications  for influence  and policing decision making would be near  none.  For this reason,  
many universities, including ARM Hub partners JCU and UQ, have developed extensive, tailored  
plans to address  this issue , these plans can be used as a guide to develop  internal guides  at any 
organisation looking to do such wo rk. 
These plans  include mitigation concepts like decentralising responsibility, reducing the risk of an 
influenced employee can affect policy undetected , and introducing vetting processes which check 
potential business partners for issues like their presen ce on  sanction lists.  As this is a continuously 
evolving challenge, dedicated staff should be assigned to develop and maintain specific action plans 
for each business unit .  
Technology Transfer  
Risk 
When dealing with suppliers in or beholden to foreign countries, there is a risk that any information 
shared with that supplier may be transferred to that country, risking a loss of control over the intellectual property. This risk often emerges when manufacturing is outsourced, exposing the 
design an d critical manufacturing data to another party.  
The consequences ca n range from a  small off- brand  competitor emerging in a foreign market, with 
limited legal redress options, to a hostile capture of all existing markets by larger, better resourced competit ors. 
Considerations  
• Viability of the product without foreign capabilities  
• Amount of inherent value in the intellectual property exported  
• Flexibility of the product design  
• Costs o f staffing supplier vetting and export control roles  
Mitigation  
The best way t o mitigate the risk of technology transfer is of course to not export it in the first place, 
but even in this case, local suppliers may leak the technology through their own  unreliable supply 
chains, especially if the significance of the technology is not adequate communicated to them . In 
many  cases, a product would simply not be viable without some degree of overseas capability being 
involved, so some risk must be assumed.  A common  practical method of mitigating this risk is to separate the design of any o utsourced 
product into several functional parts, where the low -complexity parts are outsourced, and the high -
complexity parts are manufactured locally, with focused secrecy. Since only the core component 
needs to be secured, and it is manufactured locally,  the overall cost of maintaining secrecy and 
control over the IP is far lower than trying to lock down the entire project.  
This approach makes the defensive assumption that all outsourced parts will eventually be 
transferred but lowers their effective valu e by keeping the core dependency in -house. The approach  
also relies on the product being able to be broken down into such parts (or reengineered to do so), 
and that the core dependency has a sufficiently high complexity that it cannot be quickly cloned. It  
also introduces additional manufacturing and integration costs in the local jurisdiction, which may 
defeat the purpose of outsourcing to begin with.  
This dependency approach, combined with supplier vetting, strong NDA contracting, and dedicated 
export control staff can greatly reduce the incidence of technology transfer , without requiring all 
manufacturing to be completed locally .

Task  
Assist the existing product engineering team in assessing and implementing the most appropriate 
functional safety measures for an automated cone laying truck.  
Details  
The client has designed and constructed an automated cone laying truck, that when loaded with traffic cones and driven at the appropriate speed, can lay the cones on the road at a pre -set interval.  
The automatic system consists of a pair of robotic gantry arms for pickin g up the cones from within 
the truck and placing them on the ro ad, or vice -versa, with a third gantry system inside the truck 
that brings cones from a stockpile to the arm robot working area.  
When deploying or retrieving cones, the gantry arms stick out fr om the side of the truck and pose 
several hazards to workers or pedestrians in the area due to their movement speed and end -
effector. Within the truck, the stockpiling gantry presents a hazard to workers loading cones and performing maintenance.  
Approach  
With the assistance of the ARM Hub, a functional safety assessment should first be conducted to 
assess where the most significant hazards lie  in the current iteration of the system . It is proposed 
that the optimal approach would be to conduct this interacti vely, with ARM Hub working closely on 
site with ArrowES’ Engineering team.  
From here, various mitigation  option s can be devised, whether it is a physical solution like 
implementing safety guarding and  sensors or changing the process and  scope to remove the hazard 
from this version of the system entirely. The mechanisms to be assessed will include both probabilistic and deterministic options. After safety, the mitigation choices will be driven by cost, schedule, and customer feedback.  Although ARM Hub will f ocus on the objective of safety in its 
assessment  and recommendations , oversight can be given to the technical team in determining cost 
and schedule implications of the options considered.   
Once the appropriate mitigations are decided, the ARM Hub can assist the client’s technical team in their design, implementation, and validation .  
Given the existing schedules of the client and the ARM Hub, this work should be limited to  a 
commitment of  130 hours . The work is proposed to be delivered in three consecu tive phases  (as 
described below in Deliverables) , with a schedule to be negotiated  and opportunity to review 
progress at each phase.  
 
Possible Considerations in Scope of Project  
• Add an explicit “STOP” state, complete with checked transitions and interlocks, to the 
system’s state machine. This will allow for greater safety in the maintenance and idling truck 
scenarios . 
• Add sensors to positively identify cones before grasping to help prevent accidentally 
“grabbing” pedestrians or workers. These sens ors would watch for incoming cones and only 
issue a grab command if a cone were detected. These systems would give a probabilistic 
result rather than a deterministic one, and so should be combined with other safety 
measures.  Revised proposal, 5 March 2021 ; https://advrobotics.sharepoint.com/sites/armhubprojects/shared 
documents/companies/arrowes/arrowes proposal_v4.docx  • Implement mode interlocks by ve hicle speed, disallowing the movement of the robot above 
or below a set range of speeds to prevent unforeseen circumstances at high speed and 
lower risks in the maintenance and idling truck scenarios.  
• Physical guarding like static or pop -out doors to preve nt collisions with the gantry arms.  
• Modelling to determine the failure modes of the system in situations like when an arm is hit by a passing vehicle. These scenarios would be aimed at uncovering unforeseen edge -cases.  
Deliverables  
Deliverable  1: Functional Safety Assessment  
An assessment of the system as it stands currently , with involvement  from the client’s technical 
team, aimed at identifying the hazards present and the most appropriate mitigation techniques . 
Expected time 40 hours , includi ng 5 site visits.  
Deliverable 2: Safety System Design  
ARM Hub assists the client’s technical team in designing appropriate hardware, software, and user 
interaction systems identified as most appropriate in the Functional Safety Assessment.  This includes 
design for systems like state machines, mechanical interlocks, and electrical enclosures.  
Expected time 60 hours , including  7 site visits.  
Deliverable 3: Safety System Implementation  
ARM Hub guides  and reviews  the client’s technical team in implementing the various  hardware, 
software, and user interaction systems designed in the Safety System Design . This includes guiding 
work like writing software, CAD/DFM , and the mechanical installation . This revised proposal  reduces 
the time on site during this stage of the project .  
Expected time 3 0 hours , including 3 site visits.  
Personnel

Coordination and support will be provided by Chief Operating Officer, Samuel Jesuadian.

FEASIBILITY REPORT FOR IMPROVING 
BANANA DE -HANDING WITH AUTOMATION  
 
 
 
 
 
Authors  
 
Troy Cordi e, Anthony Franze `, David Hedger , Melissa Nugent  
Advanced Robotics for Manufacturing Hub  
 
Dr Chris Lehnert  
Queensland University of Technology  
 
  
Executive Summary  
This research investigated the feasibility of developing an automating banana de -handing solution, as 
an identified labour -intensive process in Australia's banana industry. The project aimed to: define the 
challenge; assess automation technology/techniques that have been previously proposed and/or 
could be applied; provide a preliminary outline of the potential costs and benefits for pursuing 
automation; and propose a plan to progress.  
A time and motion study was undertaken over several days to define the banana de -handing 
challenge/problem by observing banana processing practices at five facilities in far north Queensland, 
recording data and interviewing management and operational staff  at these facilities. A literature 
review of research and development associated with applying automation technologies to banana de -
handing was undertaken. Relevant patented technologies were also identified. Further supplementary 
information was provided by Australian Banana Growers Council and staff of the Department of 
Agriculture and Fisheries. The findings have informed a discussion of the opportunities for 
integration/application of automation technology in banana de -handing, which could have the 
greatest potential. These are significantly different from previously proposed methods, largely due  to 
recent computer vision and robotics advances. Researchers have identified three potential options 
that could be developed with the ultimate goal of achieving  a commercial solution.  
Research outputs include d:  
-  Data collection;  
-  A desktop  study /literature review of existing technology;  
-  Definition of the problem/ challenge;  
-  Opportunities for integration of technology – three options proposed;  
-  Quantification of benchmark and technology development costs; and  
-  Project plan for further research and development.  
This project has delivered a set of conclusions and recommendations to progress automation of 
banana de -handing, based on significant evidence gathered, including a conclusive analysis of the 
current literature and related patents ; an understanding of the issues, costs, tasks and practices 
associated with a sample of banana de -handing operations ; and  knowledge of contemporary robotic, 
robotic vision and AI advancements in research including related applications. The recommendations 
take into account the fin dings that no known commercial -ready solutions exist, but that research could 
be developed towards an integrated solution. These recommendations are framed around accepted 
models of technology readiness.   
Based upon the outcomes of this feasibility study it is recommended that:  
1. Previously proposed automated de -handing solutions and inventions are unlikely to be viable 
for adoption in Australia  and do not warrant further investigation or development .  These and 
other m echanical banana de -handing technologies are likely to have unacce ptable impacts 
on fruit quality/bruising .  
2. Advancements in computer vision, machine learning and robotic handling methods provide 
promising opportunities for the development of a viable  de-handing  solution . 
3. It would be feasible to develop a solution based on the above methods to Technology 
Readiness Level 5.  4. Applied research  would enable the investigation of methods to identify the cutting trajectory  
and perform the optimal cut . 
5. Engineering services/tasks could be performed in parallel to research to test and develop  
optimise d equipment requirements (e.g., number of robotic axes required, optimal end 
effectors for cutting and handling ) and software requirements  in a like -industrial setting.  
6. Technology development could best f ocus initially  on the components that are usable across 
the potential  approaches such as computer vision, cutting devices and end effectors.  
7. In order for a minimum viable product and technical specifications for a solution to be 
developed, d etailed design of two rob otic options should be progressed to the next stage of 
development , establishing and using  a laboratory robotic cell to investigate and define 
optimal specifications  for a working  prototype . 
8. A cost-benefit  analysis would be st be conducted once the minimum viable product is specified 
and throughput can be quantified.   
9. Additional information regarding costs and requirements associated with quality , including 
current quality  impacts from de -handing and  other processing tasks would inform  both 
solution development and a cost-benefit  analysis.  
10. Commercial partners need to be identified and engaged to ensure that there is a pathway for 
the final stages of technology development and commercialisation .  
 
A project plan is attached , which identifies and estimates the time and effort (quantity and type) 
required for:  
 - the progression of two key areas of applied research that would underpin the most likely 
commercial solution: 1) best method for computer vision to determine the cutting 
trajectory; and 2) the best method to safely and effectively perform the cut.  
-  delivery of project engineering activities to develop a prototype robot cell to TRL 5, 
pending a detailed design phase and articulation of agreed technical specifications.  
This report  provides an independent assessment and body of knowledge that can be presented to key 
stakeholders, including farmers, investors and funding bodies. This can inform perceptions of the 
likelihood and appropriateness of technologies (historical, current and  emerging) for application to 
labour intensive banana de -handing processes. Further, this can inform decisions regarding 
investment in further research and development.  
 
This research was conducted by ARM (Advanced Robotics for Manufacturing) Hub in partnership with

  1 Introduction  
This research project investigates  the feasibility of automating the banana de -handing process . This 
report seeks  to provide the banana industry with an  increased  understanding o f the benefits of 
robotic s in the de-handing  proces s and what is required to progress automation.  Banana de -handing 
is a core  process at all banana processing facilities . It is a  repetitive and physically demanding activity 
which if automated , could improve processing efficiencies and provide a valuable integration point for 
robotics systems .  This research is pertinent given current  workforce reliability  and supply chain issues,  
TR4 disease , and low -cost imports threa ts. 
To understand the challenges and opportunities for integrating  robotics and automation, the research 
team conducted  time and motion stud ies in North Queensland in February 2022 , surveying  banana 
processing  at operational processing facilit ies. Farms were identified in consultation with Queensland 
University of Technology (QUT) experts, the Australian Banana Growers Council (ABGC) and Australian 
Hydraulic Services. Twelve farms were initially identified and of these , five farms took part in the study. 
Farms were identified and selected based on the following five criteria. 1) All farms were in the NQLD 
region of Innisfail/Tully which offers a mix of farms in proximity. 2) Small, medium, and large farms 
were selected t o represent automation potentials across the broader industry. 3) All farms process 
the dominant Cavendish banana variety. 4) Participating farms expressed interest in the research and 
development process and being future industry leaders. 5) Were willing to have their processes and 
labour force interviewed, audio and video recorded during regular  operating hours.  
In addition, two semi -structured interviews were conducted at each farm with a farm manager and 
banana de -hander. Australian Banana Growers Council representatives also helped to arrange a 
meeting with staff from the Department of Agriculture and Fisheries, which provided supplementary 
information. Sampling five di fferen t farms helped the researchers better understand  the nuances in 
the banana de -handing process. Moreover,  a desktop study of the literature was conducted to scope 
existing research into impro ving and automating banana de -handing and includes a review of several 
patented mechanical de -handing solutions . The data collected and analysed from the time and motion 
studies , interviews  and desktop study  inform  this data analysis and feasibility report , which incl udes 
an overview of current de-handing practice s, the identification of opportunities for integration of 
robotics , the estimated costs  of an automated solution,  conclusions and recommendations  and the 
project plan for future research & development required to progress the project . 
 
1.1 Definition of the problem/challenge.  
 
The banana industry faces significant challenges , including threats from TR4 disease and potential low -
cost imports to limitations of commercial varieties. This research project focuses specifically on the 
labour -intensive de -handing process and the potential for automation to improve production.  
Whilst automation in manufacturing, including  food production, is taking place across diverse 
industries and processes globally and automation technology is advancing rapidly, Australian banana 
producers do not have a clear view of current or emerging technologies that could be commercially 
applied to  banana de -handing. It is not clear whether technologies being applied in other industries, 
such as the use of robot arms, could meet the production requirements or be readily adapted into a 
customi sed system t hat could meet requirements. Also, the most commonly used cutting options 
need to be investigated for suitability in an automated system.  
The project team was able to define the challenge through two mechanisms:  - Observations of practices across multiple premises  
- Interviews with production managers and operational staff (de -handers).  
This provided a strong qualitative understanding of the problem/challenge with respect to current 
production environments and operations (including prioriti sation), workflow and sequencing issues 
(such as rate versus speed; sequencing between washing and sorting), product quality issues/ 
requirements/wastage, workforce issues and labour requirements/costs, cutting tools and techniques 
and other operational man agement issues that affect de -handing such as sap/bleed -time and vermin 
management. The definition obtained was sufficient to provide a basis for reviewing the literature 
regarding the application of technologies to provide an assessment of feasibility and a project plan to 
progress technology adoption.  
The following summarises  the key challenges of banana de -handing.  
• All farmers rated workforce reliability as their primary issue. Experienced de -handers are 
challenging  to find and retain.  
• It is difficult to alter the sequence of de -handing within the broader process without significant  
workflow disruptions.  
• De-handing needs to occur  near the packing shed where there is ample water supply , and it 
also has to happen between washing and before sorting.  
• The washing process is essential to remove chemicals and vermin such as snakes, bats and 
rats.  
• Banana sap has a glue -like consistency and adheres to people, tools, machinery, the fruit itself, 
resulting in a need for thorough cleaning.  
• The sap can 'bleed' every time the banana crown is cut  for approximately eight minutes.  
• Different farms have different practices to accommodate the sap, including use of tissue 
paper, washing etc.  
• Banana skin is delicate , bruises easily , and each touchpoint adds the potential risk of bruising.  
• As a result of processing, bruising can be difficult to spot before packing,  leading  to significant  
fruit rejection rates at the market.  
• De-handing is a critical task, which at times is prioriti sed by farmers.  
• Postponing other tasks can impact downstream fruit quality . For example, if bananas are not 
bagged on time, discarded fruit can increase from usual rates of 15-30% to as much as 50%.  
• Farm managers noted that d e-handing needs to happen at a consistent rate as opposed to 
outright speed. De-handers operating as fast as pos sible tended to damage more fruit and 
caused inconsist ent through put.  Factors include number of packers, number of bananas that  
the trough can take ( considering  8 minutes wash time needed ). Inconsistent throughput 
affects each stage of the downstream process.  
• Mean speeds for de-handing vary from operation to operation, dependent largely on whether 
or not de -handers are engaged in adjacent tasks.  
• Observations and evidence at the farms involved in this study indicated that no one cutting 
tool was more effective compared to another. Rather, the selection of cutting tools varied 
dependent on individual de -hander preference.  
• One exception is the de -hander's use of pneumatic knives to de -hand lady finger bananas.  
• Successful dehanding requires the hand to be cut from the stalk  approximately  one centimetre 
from a visibly prominent line where the hand joins the stalk.  
• Banana de -handers continuously adapt to natural variations in the growth of bananas. This 
variation includes tips of the banans curling back onto the stalk and obscuring its view and changes in the size and shape of the fruit. Staff reported that d e-handing injuries have 
decreased  over time , but that the task is still dangerous , as evident by the common practive 
of removing  tips from  de-handers ’ knives.  
• We were u nable to ascertain the longer term health implications of de -handing during this 
study. Factors that were mentioned at farms observed included staff rotation and contract 
duration .  
• There is a great deal of fruit damage which impacts potential use  and sale price . Based on 
farmer feedback  received , up to 50% of bananas sold are below class one, 30% or more of 
fruit is damaged but can be sold as seconds , and 15% or more is used for mulch.  
 
Limitations/exclusions: The cost and timeframe of this study limited data gathering and problem 
definition to independent observations and stakeholder perspectives at a small number of farms in a 
single region (Tully/Innisfail, far North Queensland). A com prehensive quantitative assessment of the 
banana de -handing challenge was outside the scope and sample size for this study. However, the study 
was able to quantify estimated costs per hand of current manual banana de -handing practices. In 
consultation with  ABGC, the scope of the study focused primarily on cavendish  bananas, representing 
over 90% of the banana crop in Australia. Only high -level information regarding impact of dehanding 
on fruit quality and impact on use/value of produce was gained from the interviews. As such it was 
difficult to gain a detailed understanding of this in terms of the problem definition.   
A description of practices observed at each farm is included in section two (2) of this report and 
informs the above definition of the challenge.  
Findings within the literature supported and enhanced the definition obtained through the time and 
motion study and interviews. For example, the literature review found consistency in the handling, 
tools, techniques and quality issues that need to be addre ssed when considering technology 
applications.  
 
1.2  Desktop study (literature review) of existing banana de -handing 
technology  
 
As early as 1985, Franklin identified the mechani sation of banana de -handing as a means to improv e 
banana processing in packing sheds [1].  To better understand why such devices are not commonly 
found  in banana packing sheds , it is vital to understand current practices.  In February 2022, we 
undertook a time and motion study as described in section 2.7 in conjunction with a desktop study of 
de-handing automation attempts  documented to date . Banana harvesting, de -handing and packing 
are still largely manual, repetitive and labour -intensive processes  [2].  The de -handing process occurs 
once  banana bunches have been transported to the packing shed , had their protective covers 
removed , and have entered the packing shed.  The quality of the cut during the de -handing process 
influences the subsequent grade given to the banana hand [3].  Once  bananas are de -handed, the stalk 
is discarded, and the bananas are sorted into clusters, washed and packed.  Banana de -handing is a 
repetitive and labour intensive task completed at a core integration point in banana processing  
between the field and the packing shed, making  de-handing a prime candidate for automation and 
robotics. It is anticipated that a utomating  the de -handing process would decrease manual labour and 
offer the potential to add value to downstream processes such as grading and sort ing. 
 Previous studies in improving the banana de -handing process identified risks of repetitive strain injury 
to workers’ wrist s and hands [4].  As a result of these studies , approaches were recommended to  
minimi se the risk to de -handers from all injury types.  For example, to reduce de -handers cutting 
themselves, it was recommended that de -handers use  mesh gloves on the hand supporting the  
banana  bunch and mechanical de -handers  were also explored . Other recommendations included  
improving packing sheds to allow an adequate workspace to prevent de -handers from cutting other 
operators  and reduce  repetitive strain injuries through job rotation and worker training initiatives .  
A motion study looking to quantify the repetitive strain injuries suffered by banana de -handers 
identified significant strain on workers spine s and hips in addition to their wrists and hands [5].  The 
motion study further identified the type of knife as playing a role in the injuries suffered.  The knives 
used by banana de -handers varied between standard knives, curved knives and a unique  spatula style 
knife.  While completing the motion study detailed in [5], all banana de -handers used curved knives 
(Figure 1) developed explicitly for banana de -handing [6].  The spatula style knives ( Figure 2) comprise 
a semicircle blade at the end of an extensive handle designed to keep the workers ' hand clear of the 
stalk when de -handing bananas.  The semicircle blade of the spatula style knives, like the knife 
described in the patent [7], fits the radius of the banana stalk allowing the de -hander to push the knife 
down to remove the banana hands.  The development of various task-specific knives  Has ultimately 
sought  to reduce strain on workers ’ hands, wrist s, spine and hips . Meanwhile , banana de -handing has 
remained  essentially a manual task.  
The earliest attempt identified in the literature to mechanically de -hand bananas literature was a set 
of spinning blades suspended above a tank of water designed and built -in 1985.  After removing the 
bell, dummy hands and shaping the stalk, the de -hander would lower the bunch into the spinning 
blades.  While lowering the bunch of bananas, the operator could vary the distance between the 
blades to match the stalk diameter by controlling the rotation speed of the device.  The separated 
hands would fall onto  a rotating foam pad before landing in a water bath for washing.  Familiar with 
the device, Stewart Lindsay Team Leader - Banana Production Systems with Department of Agriculture 
and Fisheries, recalls damage to the fruit was one significant hurdle to wide spread implementation of 
such a device.  Beyond damaging the fruit, the quality of the cut when removing banana hands from 
the bunch affect ed the grade and subsequent price of the fruit [3].   
Because of this quality control issue and the significant post -harvesting value of the banana crop [8], 
much of the existing literature focuses on the cutting mechanism of mechanical de -handing.

Mechanical de -handing splits into two categories, static blade and rotary cutting.  Static blade de -
handers utili se gravity or pressure from above to feed the stalk of the banana bunch through an 
adaptive blade or set of combs which remove the banana hands as the stalk progresses.  In contrast 
to passive blades, the rotary cutting de -handers use a motor to drive a cir cular blade down along the 
stalk to remove the bananas from the bunch.  . It is important to remember that cut quality needs to 
be high for ei ther approach when separating the hands from the bunch.   
 
Static blade de -handing works by suspending a bunch of bananas above a de -handing mechanism and 
lowering or pushing the bunch . As the bunch lowers , the hands of bananas are removed from the 
stalk.  While the method of de -handing the bananas is similar, the design of the cutting edge and how 
it adapts to the changing diameter of the banana stalk varies between approaches.  The ielis patent 
[9] describe s an adaptable diameter circular blade that expands  and contracts  to suit the stalk. As can 
be seen in  the patent drawings provided ( Figure 6), four quarter -circle blades slotted into the 
neighbouring blade while a sprung linkage maintain eds contact with the banana stalk . 
The patent by Zhou [10] describes a set of five comb style blades connected via a pivoting linkage 
(Figure 10).  Each comb attaches to the pivoting joint with a spring allowing adaption to the stalk's 
diameter.  Work to optimi se the comb style banana de -handers ( Figure 5) explored many variables in 
the mechanism, including the number, size and shape of combs, the size of the thin cutting linkages 
and the speed at which the cutting was performed [3].  The banana de -handing device described in 
[11] and subsequent patent application [12] describe d a seven -bar linkage combed blade ring.  The 
ring, capable of expanding to a diameter of 164mm and compressing to 43mm , comprises six combs 
and a constant force component ( Figure 8). As the combs remove d the hands, the constant force 
component maintains the mechanism's contact with the banana stalk. Work described by Duan in 
patent [13] decreases the effort and time to de -hand a bunch of bananas.  The mechanism consists of 
three pairs of combs linked with two cutting links that create the circular cutting ring.  The mechanism 
is mounted on top of a movable work surface. The worksurface can raise and drop, and by raising the 
mechanism and banana bunch the dropping action force d the bunch through the cutting combs.   
Static blade de -handers use d pressure from above or gravity to push the bananas through a series of 
cutting combs and links t o remove the banana hands from the bunches.  Application of  these devices 
show ed them to be functional and create clean cuts when removing the hands.  
  
 
The rotary cutting de -handers use a circular rotating blade, as the name suggests.  The stalk passes 
through the blade's centre.  The review found two approaches: a handheld device lowered over the 
bunch and a static device with the bananas lowered through  it.  The device created by Shravan and 
seen in the video [14] shows a handheld rotary banana de -hander.  The prototype device is lowered 
over the banana stalk removing the banana hands.  The demonstrated device is cumbersome and 
inadvertently removes individual bananas from the hands,  a non -desirable trait.  The patented rotary 
type banana combing machine  described in [15] shows a similar motor configuration driving a pully to 
spin a cutting edge.

The rotary type banana combing machine spins a pair of knives that can vary in their distance to adapt 
to the diameter of the banana bunch stalk.  This de -handing device is mounted on a workbench and is 
fed from the top. As described in Zhou’s patent  [16], The ability to vary the diameter of the cutter is 
an essential part of maintaining the quality of the cut when removing banana hands.   The variable -
diameter self -adaptive rotary banana bunch cutter consists of  eighteen comb -style  blades ( Figure 7).  
The diameter between the blades is variable to ensure clean cuts when removing banana hands from 
bunches. Rotary cutting banana de -handing mechanisms spin the blades used to cut the banana hands 
from the bunch.  
One de -handing device that did not fall into the fixed blade  or rotary cutting types was the fretsaw 
banana de -hander ( Figure 10) [17].  The fretsaw banana de -hander uses a fretsaw and clamp to hold 
the banana bunches and remove the hands.  The clamp positioned below the saw holds the bunch in 
place by grasping the stalk when the saw is engaged to remove the hand.   
The findings of the literature review suggest that a  successful banana de -handing automation solution 
will need to adapt to the tapering diameter of banana stalks to achieve the clean -cut produced by 
current manual banana de -handing practices.  
Paired with banana de -handing are also mechanisms for holding or grasping banana bunches.  The 
farms  observed in this current study used a chain looped back on itself that pull ed tight under gravity 
to hang the bananas .  This review found two patents for clamping devices from the South China 
Agricultural University (SCAU).  The first such device [18] is a reversible self -locking clamp ( Figure 11) 
using a pair of screws to actuate the mechanism.  The second patent describes a similar self -locking 
device with an over centre latch ( Figure 9) to actuate the clamp [19].  Similarly, the work in [20] 
explore s automatic pneumatic clamping and detaching of the banana stem.  Autonomous attaching 
and detaching of the banana stem during the de -handing process remove s one manual task from the 
de-handers workload.

Despite developments in the use of computer vision for assessing quality to support grading and 
sorting in related applications /crops , the literature review found limited investigation of the use of 
computer vision to support automation in banana de -handing .  Computer vision has been used for 
the detection of bananas in the paddock as necessary for banana harvesting robots [24].  This ability 
to segment the hands of bananas using colour and texture base d features could be adapted for use 
in the de -handing processes and value add in the sorting and grading of bananas.  Multiple 
approaches exist to identify banana stalk s in the paddock for robotic gripper grasping.  M. Chen 
proposes using stereo cameras to identify the banana stalk and generate a 3D model ( Figure 13) 
[25].  
While T. Chen has developed a deep neural network to identify banana bunch stalks [26].  Literature 
exploring computer vision in banana harvesting has demonstrated an ability to segment banana 
bunches and stalks in the paddock.  These existing approaches could be adapted for banana grasping 
and de-handing and offer the opportunity to add value  to the process  in the packing shed .  
Banana de -handing remains a repetitive, labour -intensive process that can pose a risk to worker 
safety.  The removal of banana hand s from bunch es upon arrival to the packing shed has been 
identified as a bottleneck in the processing of bananas . This review looked at existing literature and 
patents regarding  banana de -handing.  The literature identifies two mechanical banana de -handing 
approaches: static blade de -handing and rotary cutting de -handing.  The static blade de -hands the 
bunch utili sing gravity or pressure from above to push the banana bunches through a set of variable 
diameter cutting combs and links.

As part of this feasibility report for improving banana de -handing through robotics , we observed

variances were observed in the approach that employee s took to  completing the task.  
A brief overview of the shared process is detailed below.  Once the bananas were de -handed , the 
hands were clustered by separating into  groups of approximately five to six  bananas. Once clustered , 
the bananas move d along a conveyor belt to the sorters . The sorters manually separate d the 
bananas based on the size and quality of the fruit. The sorted fruit  continue d to the packers  who  
load ed the bananas into cartons . The cartons were loaded onto pallets for storage and ripening.  
 
 
A greater understanding of banana de -handing was gained by observing the process undertaken at

We observed the banana de-handing process in fi ve different packing facilities in the Innisfail/Tully 
region of North Queensland, Australia.  Part of the c riteria we used for selecting  farms  was different 
approaches to banana processing. Although we observed variations in processing practices at each 
of the farms and their packing facilities (or sheds)  we visited , a core set of tasks was completed at all 
sheds .  
Approaches that varied  included processing quantity, processing style , wheel or trough , and the 
number of employ ees in the shed. As a result , we observed that each packing shed's de -handing 
process was tailored to the shed layout, number of processing lines,  and the quantity of fruit 
handled. We observed de-handers operating as individuals and displaying clear team -based 
strategies to effectively remove banana hands from bunches . While each shed had a different 
approach , a clear set of tasks w as complet ed. 
Every packing shed we visited completed the same core steps during the banana de -handing 
process. These clear and repeatable tasks observed across the sample  of banana packing facilities in 
Innisfail and Tully will form the basis for our proposals for inclusion of robotics in banana de -
handing.  
1. The b anana bunch arrives at the de-handing area , following a bunch wash,  either by 
chain or gantry.  
2. The desired cut location is identified by the de-hander  (approx. 1cm from abscission 
line) . 
3. Individual hands are cut and removed  by a labourer . 
4. Hands are placed in the trough or on the wheel.  
a. At this stage , varying amounts of discarding damaged fruit, clustering and 
sorting is completed by the de-handers.  
b. At this stage sap is washed from the cut banana  hands . 
5. Repeat from step two until all hands are removed . 
6. Discard the banana stalk.  
7. Perform tidying  tasks such as organi sing the overhead chains .  
8. Repeat from step one.
