3  Opportunities for  the integration of robotics.  
 
Recent advancements in robotics and computer vision systems were considered along  with the 
literature findings and on -site observation to assess the potential for a  viable  robotic de -handing 
solution to be developed . Although robotics has allowed for the automation of many tedious and 
dangerous tasks, the natural variation across banana bunches has traditionally hindered automation 
and robotic solutions. Contemporary computer vision systems allow for more adaptable r obotics, 
accounting for variation in robotic  environment s and task s. We propose a shift away from complex 
mechanical approaches to a robotic de -handing solution as applications of robotic systems have 
been found  to offer the following benefits:  
1. Process quality : Robots can support a consistent level of quality, irrespective of external 
stressors of the organi sation.  2. Addressing l abour variability : Robots can work mostly without downtime; however, they 
require routine maintenance to function at optimal levels.  
3. Scalability:  Once the robotic process has been implemented and infrastructure put in place, 
the number of robots can easily be increased to scale with demand.  
4. Increased competitiveness:  Adopting robots enables Australia to compete with  countries 
with  lower labour rates.  
5. Labour cost for output : Using robots, the manufacturing cost does not necessarily increase 
interrelated  to output, as it traditionally does for manufacturing processes that  rely on 
predominantly manual processes.  
Earlier  attempts to automate banana de -handing , seen in the desktop study , used complex 
mechanical solutions.  The proposed solutions  used complex sets of comb style kni ves and linkages to 
adapt to the size and shape of the banana stalk. Observations in banana packing facilities  indicated 
that such a solution would require continual sharpening  of the blades and sap removal  from moving 
parts . A robotic solution coupled with computer vision could provide an alternative strategy that 
allow s customi sed remov al of each banana hand. By id entifying the cut  location with computer 
vision , a robot arm could accurately remove each hand from the bunch.  Robotics coupled with 
computer vision could allow a daptability to natural v ariation in banana bunches without the 
complexity of multiple cutting edges and linkages.  
We observed a clear set of steps required to remove a hand of bananas from a bunch.  The gantry 
brough t banana  bunches to the de-handing area . Each hand was removed individua lly and placed in 
the trough/wheel , and the de -hander discarded the banana  stalk.  The repeatability of the tasks to 
de-hand bananas make s it a prime can dida te for automation.  While the natural variation  in the 
bunches make s compliant systems complex and difficult to implement , robotics coupled with 
computer vision could be expected to handle the  variation.   
The data analysis of the banana de -handing operations showed a considerable amount of downtime 
and v ariation in the time to  remove a hand of bananas from a bunch.  A robot can continue to 
operate at a consistent pace and with consistent quality without breaks and downtime . This 
consistency would supply the downstream process with fruit and free up banana de-hander 
resources to complete other tasks.  One of the significant  benefits of robotics is producing  consistent 
results constantly . 
In addition to our observations of the banana de-handing process , we observed ma rkings on the 
banana bunch es that are ideal visual markers for a robotic banana de-hander.  The abscission  line 
(Figure 24) is an ideal  reference point for cutting the hands from the bunch. Using computer vision , 
the abscission  line could be located for each hand . With the l ine's location, the robot can calculate a 
cutting trajectory leaving the desired amount of wood , and t he robot arm would then cut the hand 
from the bunch. While our observations are not absolute, we are confident that the abscission line 
exists on all cavendish bananas  (Figure 25) and visually defines  where the bract attaches to the 
bunch. Our observations indicate that the abscission line remains on the bunch once the bract drops 
off. One cha llenge with this approach is instances of banana hands curling towards the s talk and 
blocking the view of the line. Currently , banana de -handers would push the bananas away from the 
stalk to cut the hands from the bunch. A de -handing robot may need to replicate this motion of 
clearing the hands from the stalk .

With the knowledge gathered regarding banana de -handing, we propose developing an approach 
that uses robotics coupled with computer vision to automate the  process. We deviate from the

reasons that we suggest these strategies for developing an automated solution should be furthe r

3.1 Automation Options  
 
Three potential  options that could be developed for automating  banana de -handing are presented . 
The three approaches proposed  are based on the observations made  in Innisfail/Tully and 
information uncovered in the desktop review. The three proposals distinguish themselves from 
previous  attempts to automate banana de-handing by leveraging recent robotics and computer 
vision advances . Robotics paired with computer vision is an approach that could be expected to  
allow individual tailoring of the solution for each banana bunch.   
3.1.1 Option 1 The robotic  banana de -hander  
 
This robot could work in the existing space for the banana de-handers .  It would be  mounted on a 
track for movement and equipped with a perception  module  and two robot arms.   The first robot 
arm could use a purpose -designed and built robot gripper to grasp banana hands and position the 
bunch .  The second arm , equipped with one of the cutting implements described below , would  cut 
the hand from the stalk.   Once a hand is removed from the bunch , the robot  would place them in the 
trough/wheel.  
This approach represents a significant investment in both research and development  – the largest 
investment of the three options proposed in this report . Note : a variant of this robot might be able 
to use a single more complex robot arm and man ipulator combination  (i.e. the cutter and grasping 
tool on one arm). However, this would pose additional challenges in design .

requirements , including separating it from other banana workers . 
The robotic banana de -hander rep resents the most signi ficant investment in research and 
development of all the options presented. The timeline for technology such as custom manipulators 
and software to mature for com merc ial implementation is anticipated to  be from  five to ten  years. 
This solution  offers broad opportunit ies for integration into the downstream workflow. Future 
technologies required for a robotic banana de -hander , including the manipulator and cutting tool , 
apply to the clustering, sorting,  and banana  packing tasks . A robot similar to the robotic banana de-

with the proposed de -handing manipulator could be further developed to pack banana clusters . 
Additionally , If an alternative to washing the sap from banana clusters can be found, a single robotic 
banana worker could de-hand, sort/cluster and pack banan as. The robotic banana de -hander 
represents the most ambitious approach to de -handing banana bunches proposed . The 
development of required components for its success do es have potential impl ementations in other 
aspects of banana processing  as well as processing of other foods .   
3.1.2 Option 2 The submersion de-hander  
The proposed  submersion de-hander lifts the banana bunch out of a trough and removes the hands 
at the water level. The submersion de-hander uses a robot arm, a lifting and positioning mec hanis m, 
a perception package and one of the cutting methods detailed below.  The submersion de-hander 
could be  a standalone industrial robotic solution or operate alongside one or more  de-hander s in a 
cobotic solution.  
As the banana bunch arrives on the overhead rail , the bunch is attached to the lifting and positioning 
mechanism and lowered into the tank. Once fully submerged , the lifting and positioning  mechanism 
lifts the bunches out of the tank . As the bunch rises out of the tank, the perception system identifies 
each  hands a nd location for the cut. The robot arm cuts the hand from the bunch . Once removed 
from the bunch, the hand is moved away with a water jet.  There is no additional requirement to 
handle the banana b ecause the hands  are removed at water level.  The process is repeated  for each 
hand on the bunch , with the lifting and positioning mechanism adjusting to the location of the cut . A 
conveyor lifts the hands from the tank onto the trough/wheel. Future work could see an additional 
module for clustering and sorting bananas before entering  the trough/wheel.

bunch attachment. Finally , the entire de-handing process could be automated.

hander. The submersion de -hander offers a staged approach to the automation of banana de -

results can be seen in banana packing sheds.

The tank used to de -hand the banana bunches from below will be located in the banana de-handing

mechanical system to position the bunch for the lifting mechanism or the addition of an actuator.  
De-handing banana bunces  from below simplifies the post -cutting process  by removing the hands 
directly into the water. Cutting the hands directly into the water removes the need for an additional

of a cobotic  solution. The operator could assist in positioning the bunch into the lifting  mechanism 
before the robot de -hands the bunch.  The approach would simplify the modification needed for the 
attachment of bunches. This cobotics approach would see a single banana de -hander operate 
multiple submersion de -handers.  
The ability to incorporate robotic collaboration into the de-handing from below approach  means 
that we can stage its development. Starting with the operator helping align and maneuver the bunch

The modular nature of the proposed  approach to remove hands from below means future work

5 Conclusions & Recommendations   
During this project, we visited a representative set of banana packing facilities in north Queensland 
and conducted a desktop study of existing literature. We have found that banana processing remains 
a labour -intensive process , with the manual de -handing component providing an additional  risk of 
working with and near knives along with repetitive strain injuries to hips and hands.  Within the 
literature, existing attempts to mechani se and automate banana de -handing have utili sed complex 
mechanical systems. These systems are susceptible to banana sap , and at least one system was not 
continued due to causing fruit damage.   
Banana de -handing is a repetitive task completed at a core integration point in banana processing 
which makes de -handing a prime candidate for automation and robotics.  At each of the packing 
sheds , we identified a core set of  de-handing  tasks:  
1. The banana bunch arrives at the de -handing area either by chain or gantry.  
2. Individual hands are removed from the bunch.  
3. Hands are placed in troughs or on a wheel conveyor system.  
4. The tasks then repeat from step two until all hands are removed.  
5. Banana stalks are discarded.  
6. Perform tiding tasks such as organi sing the overhead chains.   
7. Repeat step one.  
We have proposed three possible robotic approaches to improve the banana de -handing process. 
Robots can support a consistent level of quality, irrespective of external stressors of the 
organi sation. Productivity/Speed: Robots can work mostly without downtime, holidays or sick leave; 
however, they require routine maintenance to function at optimal levels.  
Based upon the outcomes of this feasibility study it is recommended that:  
1. Previously proposed automated de -handing solutions and inventions are unlikely to be 
viable for adoption in Australia and do not warrant further investigation or development.   
These and other mechanical banana de -handing technologies are likely to have 
unacceptable impacts on fruit quality/bruising.  
2. Advancements in computer vision, machine learning and robotic handling methods provide 
promising opportunities for the development of a viable de -handing solution.  
3. It would be feasible to develop a solution based on the above methods to Technology 
Readiness Level 5.  
4. Applied research would enable investigation of methods to identify the cutting trajectory and 
maneuvering required to perform the optimal cut.  
5. Engineering services/tasks could be performed in parallel to research to test and develop 
optimised equipment requirements (e.g. number of robotic axes required, optimal end 
effectors for cutting and handling) and software requirements in a like -industrial setting.  
6. Technology development could best focus initially on the components that are usable across 
the potentail approaches such as computer vision, cutting devices and end effectors.  7. In order for a minimum viable  product and technical specifications for a solution to be 
developed, detailed design of two robotic options should be progressed to the next stage of 
development , establishing and using a laboratory robotic cell to investigate and define 
optimal specifications for a working prototype.  
8. A cost benefit analysis would best be conducted once the minimum viable product is specified 
and throughput can be quantified.  
9. Additional information regarding costs and requirements associated with quality, including 
current quality impacts from de -handing and other processing tasks would inform both 
solution development and a cost benefit analysis.  
10. Commercial partners need to be identified and engaged to ensure that there is a pathway for 
the final stages of technology development and commercialisation.

  Project Overview  
The aim of this project was to design and develop an autonomous laundry handling system that 
could help close the autonomy gap s in commercial laundries .  
Consolidated Linen Service (CLS) is a commercial laundry company operating three laundries in 
Hervey Bay, Gladstone, and Airlie Beach. At the onset of the pandemic, their business was heavily 
impacted by the decline of the tourism sector. Together with the ARM Hub, they applied for and 
receiv ed a grant under the Essential Goods and Supply Chain program run by the Queensland 
Government  to help alleviate the effects on their business .  
This grant allowed the ARM Hub to begin work on a system that would help automate some of the processes within a commercial laundry, with a view to wide deployment of the system across all of 
CLS’ locations. The automation  would in turn allow CLS to be more flexible in uncertain times, upskill 
their staff from manual labourers to automation operators, and boost tot al productivity once 
tourism returned to its peak.  
The focus of this project became the towel unfolding task , which is where towels that have been 
dried in an industrial drier and collected in a hopper must be unfolded and fed flat into a folding 
machine. This is one of the last remaining  heavily  manual task s in the laundry , requiring the operator 
to disentangle a towel from a large pile, find the corners, stretch the towel out, and place it flat onto 
a conveyor belt that takes it away to the folder. This p rocess takes place every 6 seconds, in an 
environment that can get up to 50 degre es Celsius and around 95% relative humidity , requiring 
workers to take regular hydration and rest breaks . 
D el i verabl es  
The ARM Hub team made use of recent developments in the global computer vision and machine learning fields to develop a robotic system capable of detecting and manipulating the corners of towels. This system fills the autonomy gap in laundries by enabling automatic handling of towelling 
and presents a promising development path towards widespread commercialisation around 
Australia and the w orld.   
• Computer vision system capable of detecting  the edges and corners of soft objects  
• Machine learning pipeline to rapidly generate training data with depth sensors

Exi sti ng Commerci al Soluti ons 
Commercial solutions for automating the towel unfolding task are available from several large 
laundry equipment suppliers. Notably, Jensen Group have developed two separate systems using 
different principles.  
The Jensen Evolution Cube ( https://youtu.be/MZAiIk2_vuI ) uses linear manipulators to drag towels 
over a set of mandrels to progressively expose their corners. The Jensen Evolution Spider (
https://youtu.be/AmK48ep2lUg ) initially stretches the towel out with a linear manipulator and uses 
a computer vision system to identify the ends. A pair of cartesian robotic arms then grabs the ends 
of the towel and holds it over a moving  conveyor which exposes the hanging corners by dragging 
them out. Both systems then use a set of conveyor belts to fully stretch out the towel before 
delivering it to the next machine.  
Feedback from the client indicat ed that neither  of these systems have seen  much  commercial 
adoption, and that they  have a reputation for unreliability and low throughput.  There does not seem 
to be much in the way of technical data available for these systems, and the lack of widespread 
commercial adoption may explain this.  
Single  Arm  Unfolding  
A paper titled Unfolding an item of rectangular clothing using a single arm and an assistant 
instrument  (Yuba & Yamakazi, 2014)  describes a method of unfolding a towel that is grasped by a 
single arm, by grab bing the corner of the towel and dragging it over a device mounted to the corner 
of a table. The device acts as a sort of die or mandrel that tries to spread the towel out, getting in between the folds.  
This research shows  that it is possible to fully unfold a towel with a single robot arm relatively 
reliably but  using this method  may run into  physical workspace limitations . The idea would be worth 
pursuing if the cost of additional robotics outweighs the space require ment.  
Dual Ed g e  Cla s s ific a tio n  
A paper titled Dual edge classifier for robust cloth unfolding (Gabas, Kita, & Yoshido, 2021) . shows a 
method for grabbing the adjacent corners of a held towel corner using computer vision and dee p 
learning techniques. The authors note  a successful grab rate between 8 0% and 95% depending on 
the item tested , which would  be a perfectly usable result in a production system with error checking.  
The most promising aspect of this paper is that it outline s the use o f a RGB and depth camera to 
collect training data of a towel with green painted edges held by a single robot gripper. The edges of the towel are segmented using the RGB data and this is then used as the ground truth to train a 
classifier that us es only dep th information. This means that a large amount of training data can be 
automatically generated with the painted towel, without requiring that any towels are painted in the 
final system since the depth camera does not consider colours.  
This metho d of data collection minimises what is traditionally the most labour- intensive element of 
deep learning methods, which means we can take advantage of the flexibility and power of deep learning models without having to invest as much time in development as other optio ns. 
 
 Planni ng  
At the beginning of the project, the team generated several proposals for a towel unfolding system , 
focusing on  the properties of a rectangular towel when hung or pulled by a corner. The central 
challenge  was that  to unfold a towe l, two adjacent corners must be grasped, rather than those 
opposite one another.   
It was observed that  when  a towel was hung up by a corner, the opposite corner would usually  be at 
the lowest point. When these two corners were grasped and stretched apart  horizontally, the 
remaining two corners would usually hang at the new lowest point, either one of which could now 
be grabbed to end up with two adjacent corners.   
A quick prototype system taking advantage of these properties  was assembled , aiming to replicate 
the hanging and corner grabbing steps by lying the towel on a table and stretching it out to simulate gravity. By lying the towel on a table, the ste ps could be performed sequentially, without needing 
two arms , and without needed the computer vision o r analytic s used in the Yuba paper . 
The setup used  a Universal Robots UR10 six-axis robot ic arm fitted with a Robotiq 2F -85 two -finger 
gripper , and a set of clamps and cork blocks . The cork blocks were set up  on the edge  of the table to 
form a sort of die or mandrel, similar in use to th e device in the Yuba paper . The robot was 
presented with the corner of a towel, which it grabbed and then dragged through the block setup, 
which offered a resistance like  hanging under gravity .

Since this prototype had only consumed a couple of days of project time, the  team presented the

1. continue development of this table -based system until it is commercially viable, regardless 
of performance issues ;  
2. develop the table -based system but focus on custom robotic hardware and optimising the

The client chose the third option , and so a new system was planned. The aim was to avoid wh at the

and machine learning in a way that was designed to  maxim ise the potential through put and

Computer V i si on 
The Realsense  cameras combine an RGB camera and 3D LIDAR  sensor , generating an image with 
both RGB and depth information for each pi xel. These cameras are used in two main operations, 
furthest point detection and corner detection.  
Furthest point detection refers to the process of generating a point cloud of a given area, sorting the points by  their distance  along a given vector , then c hoosing one of the  points furthest along.  The 
point chosen is 100 points away from the end of the list to ensure any unfiltered noise  does not 
affect the result. Since each point cloud  consists of 768,000 points, this does not significantly affect 
the real -world location of the detected point.  
This method  used  twice in the  unfolding sequence ; to find the highest point in the towel container 
and the lowest point of an unknown towel when it is first presented.  To prevent detection of the 
towel container or th e robotic arms, the obtained point clouds are first cropped down to the area 
where towels are expected to be found.  
The corner detection operation consists of three  steps, pre-processing, edge classification, and 
corner classification.  Since the system sho uld be invariant to the colour of the towel, only the depth 
information  is used for the proces s, so the first step of pre -processing is to discard the RGB 
information from the camera , followed by  a combination of  Canny edge detection and some filtering 
and line thinning passes. The result is  a binary image that shows the most significant changes in  
depth visible on the towel, including the shape of the towel against the background and any visible 
folds.  The image is finally reshaped and rescaled to fit into  the convolutional neural network (CNN) 
in the next step.  
The edge classification algorithm is  based on the technique described in the Gabas  paper mentioned 
earlier, which consists of a CNN  based on the U -Net architecture that operates on the entire pre-
processed  image . The CNN is  designed to detect the so -called “real” edges of the towel, 
differentiating them from the folds that are also highlighted in the pre -processing step .  
Labelled data  was obtained by painting the edges of a white towel in green and using the discarded 
RGB data to generate a mask o f “real” vs folded edges.  This towel was presented to a recording 
Realsense camera in the grip of a UR10  in a similar manner to the final workspace setup, and slowly 
rotated and repositioned  to generate 3000  training images.  The model was then trained for several days, testing a variety of kernel sizes, number of layers, 
learning rates , and augmentation techniques for the best results.  The output of the CNN is a pixel -
wise classification of the detected edg es in the input image .  
The final step is to take t he detected edges and determine whether they constitute a “real” corner. 
This uses an algorithm also described in the Gabas  paper , which first detects the left and right- most 
points of the image , which are  presumed to be corners, and then counts the number  and type of the 
edges that pass through that point. In this implementation, a small circle is drawn around the corner in question and used as a mask for the classified image. The blobs of pixels formed by  this operation 
are averaged and then  sampled for  their edge type (“real” or fold) then  counted . 
The result for each corner can be classified as follows: A “real” corner will have exactly two “real” edges intersecting it, and no fold edges ; a towel corner that is folded forward will have two “real” 
edge an d one-fold edge; a towel corner that is folded backwards will have one “real” edge and one-
fold edge”; any other combination of edges can be classified as unknown. This information can be 
used to determine whether a “real” edge is visible, or whether the towel could be rotated to expose 
one that is folded forward or backwards.

node -oriented communication middleware. Multiple individual  software nodes  are assigned to 
collect data from the sensors and send commands to  the robotic system s, while a core node 
arranges  the communication between the m.

vision and schedul er systems and the other for controlling the robotic systems. This was done  to

The system is coordinated  by the scheduler no de, which runs through a sequence  of actions 
determined  by the current system state.  These actions include collecting and processing camera 
images, moving the robot arms to various waypoints, and actuating the grippers.  For development 
purp oses, the action s can either be manually  triggered , or automatically called in sequence.  
Each Realsense camera connects to the workstation via a USB3.1 connection and is managed by a 
node  running a custom driver based on the Intel pyrealsense2 library. Thi s driver sets up  the 
cameras, captures the RGB and depth information,  aligns the images spatially,  creates a point cloud 
from the depth information, then publishes a ROS message containing all this  information  once per 
second.  The scheduler node captures  these image messa ges and caches them until processing is 
required  (either looking for the furthest point or a grabbable corner) . 
Most of the nodes in the robot control container form parts of the MoveIt robotic planning stack. 
MoveIt provides a generic waypoint movement in terface  using ROS  which the scheduler node sends 
point move commands to. These commands are passed on to the cho sen planner running in the 
planner node, which in this case is the Pilz Industrial Motion Planner, running in linear point -to-point 
mode.  This i s a relatively conservative planner that attempts to keep the end effector moving in a straight line whe never po ssible  and should produce deterministic movement plans between two 
predetermined waypoints , reducing the risk of collision . 
The movement plans a re passed to a robot controller node which is based on  the Universal Robots 
ROS Driver and modified to support c ommunication with two arms at once.  It communicates with 
the UR10s  over a set of TCP ports, sending movement commands and receiving position inf ormation 
which is passed back to the planner node . The Robotiq grippers are con trolled by a node based on 
Danfoa’s Robotiq 2finger g rippers library, which takes simple open and close commands for each 
gripper from the scheduler and passes on a desired posi tion to the gripper using Modbus over an 
USB to RS485 converter.  Sequence

To begin the unfolding operation, the scheduler node is booted in automatic mode. From her e it will 
reset the workspace by opening both grippers and commanding both arms to return to a “home” 
position . 
The first step is to image the towels in the container with the Realsense camera mounted on it . The 
point cloud is run through the furthest poin t algorithm to find the highest point in the container, 
which is assumed to be a towel. The left arm is then commanded to move to this point and close its grabber.  The arm then raises the towel out of the container and, following a set of predetermined 
waypoints, moves to a position where the towel is visible to the bench -mounted  camera, and fully 
reachable by the other arm.   
At this  stage it is unknown what state the grabbed  towel is in ; whether it is being held loosely by a 
single corner, bunched up,  in a bundle with multiple towels, or not present at all due to a grab or 
vision failure.  The scheduler then images the towel with the bench -mounted camera and calls the 
furthest point algorithm again to determine the lowest point in set region of space wh ere the towel 
should be.  
If the algorithm finds no points, the towel is likely not there at all , and the scheduler  opens the 
grippers and  restarts the operation. In every other case however, the lowest point in this region can 
be assumed to be the corner of a towel , and so the right arm is now commanded to move to this 
point and close its grabber.  
The left arm now opens  its gripper and moves o ff to the left, out of the way , while the right arm lifts 
the towel by the corner it has grabbed and presents i t to the bench mounted camera.  The towel at 
this point should be hanging loosely by a corne r and the corner detection routine can begin.  
The bench -mounted camera now takes an image of the towel and calls the corner detection 
algorithm to determine if the leftm ost p oint of the hanging towel is a “real” corner and grabbable by 
the left arm. If not, the right arm is rotated slightly into a new position, aiming to expose a new side 
of the towel to the camera, and the process repeats  up to two more  times. If a grabb able corner is 
not detected after these attempts, the towel is dropped and the operation is restarted, but if one is 
detected, then the left arm is commanded to move to that corner and grab it . 
The scheduler now  calculates the side len gth of the towel between t he two  grabbed  corners and 
moves the left arm upwards  and leftwards  to a point that distance away from the right arm, 
stretching the towel out flat. The system can then image the towel a final time report on whether 
the towel is suitably  flat. The system t hen drops the towel and the cycle repeats.  
Re sults  
After several days of incremental testing t he system  software was committed , and the prototype  
was set up to automatically run through 5 unfolding attempts at a time .  
After 50 attempts,  it successfully un folded a grabbed towel approximately 25% of the time.  In 2 
cases (4% of attempts) the system reported a successful unfolding operation, but the towel was not 
flat due to a computer vision false positive.  In roughly 10% of cases, the oper ation was aborted e arly 
due to a failed grab , due to either vision system o r gripper malfunction  (discu ssed below) . In the 
remaining  attempts, a suitable corner for grabbing was not identified.  
The motion planning system performed well throughout t his testing , ensuring the m otion was linear 
and predictable  without generating  any configurations that the robotic arms could not reach.  At the 
speed allowed, the full cycle time of the system when a suitable corn er is not iden tified is 2 minutes. 
A successf ul grab on the first atte mpt results in a cycle time of 1.5 minutes.  
The feedback from the client was extremely positive. To quote CLS Operations Director Tom Roberts , 
“We think [the solution] has huge pot ential in every laundry to increase their efficiencies and safety 
and thro ughput  so that is where we want to get to a point where its commonplace to have our 
solution in the laundry industry ”  Dis c u s s io n  
While t he overall success rate for the system to unf old a given towel  (25%) was lower than the ~ 85% 
achieved in the Gabas pape r, the  vision system correctly identified a grabbable corner with  a false 
positive rate of only 20%, which is far better than random chance. This implies that the limits to the 
performance of the system a re more to do with the failure of the  robotic  system  to provide corner 
candidates to the vision system , and that the vision system  itself is suitable for the task.  
In the context of a  future  fully automated  unfolding system, the final flatness check captured by the 
bench -mounted camera would be able to stop  these false- positive  towel s from proceeding to 
downstream processes like an  automatic folder.  
Since t he primary bottleneck to the overall success rate was that there were often no suitable 
corners presented to the left arm for it to grab. The left arm is only capable of grabbing corners that 
are presented on the left side of the towel, and so misses any cor ners visible on the right. 
Additionally, the right arm is constrained in its range of motion at full extension to around 180 
degrees, which can mean tha t some corners are never exposed.  
This could be mitigated in the future by rearranging the workspace suc h that the towel is accessible 
from all sides, and the right arm is able to rotate the towel more freely, to expose more potential corners to the vision  system. Additionally, since t he bench -mounted camera only captures images 
from one aspect of the towel, several more cameras  could be added so that  more grab opportunities 
could be detected.  
It was observed that due to the arrangement of the arms when pa ssing the towel from the left arm 
to the right arm , the towel often folds up on itself such that the c orners are tucked inside and are 
not visible no matter the rotation. This could be solved by augmenting the rotation step with a shake or rotation in mult iple axes.  
Ultimately these issues all seemingly stem from the workspace setup and available equipment 
limitations rather than any procedural elements of the system . These issue s are noted so that 
appropriate steps  can be taken in the design of any follow -up system .  
The primary advancement noted  by the team  would be to mount the robot arms either on their 
sides or  to suspend  them  upside down , which would recover a large amount of the workspace that is 
currently unusable . This would allow much more freedom  of movement  for the arms and  allow for 
much tighter setup of the camera systems . 
The vision  system was only trained using one towel but handled a variety of sizes equally well. With 
significantly more training data and deep learning model development, the  computer vi sion system 
could likely be improved to achieve performance like  that achieved in the Gabas  paper.  
The linear speed of the arms was limited to below 0.1m/s for safety and  could easily be increase d by 
a factor of four (giving a cycle time of roughly 3 0 seconds)  without excessive risk , but much faster 
cycle times  would be limited by the  high travel distance required in the current workspace 
arrangement.  An ideal system for the current client would achieve a cycle time of under 6  seconds  to 
replicate current capacity . The specification of robotic arms  dedicated to the task  with limited 
degrees of freedom , simpler  end effectors , and a better workspace layout  would all help  drop  the 
cycle time significantly.   
The cycle times were also somewhat  limited by the computer vision elements ; the furthest point 
algorithm takes around half a second to run, while the corner detection algorithm takes about one second.  These speeds  could readily be increased with the addition of more compute power or by 
cutting the resolution of the vision system to the minimum required.  
Another issue is that the vision system must  wait for the towel to become relatively stationary in 
order to su pply an accurate grab coordinate. This is not an issue for the towels in the container, but 
whenever a towel is presented, the system must  wait  several seconds  for the towel to settle, or else 
take several images in a row and take the average.  This issue  could be mitigated by either adding an 
anti-sway algorithm to the robotic co ntrol system, or by running the computer vision system fast 
enough that it can predict the period of the oscillation.  
In testing, the cases where the gripper failed to grab the to wel, either in the container or while 
hanging from an  arm,  tended to be caused by the movement of the gripper. Th e Robotiq grippers 
use two rubber pads that move towards one another, remaining parallel but moving forward 
throughout the closing process.  
This gripping action is suboptimal, as it changes the effective grab point dep ending on where in the 
stroke the gripper first encounters th e towel. The large pads can push the towel out of position 
before fully closing  and can get caught up on other parts of the towel, compromising the strength of 
the grab.  In a custom -built  system,  the grippers  could use a much smaller, toothed finger system  
that would retain the towel if it encountered it too early.  
Many of the decisions made about the design of the prototype were made to make the best use of 
available resources, including the use  of the UR10 arms and Robotiq grippers. Designing a more 
suitable workspace with robotic systems specified deliberately for the task would be the highest 
priority in any follow -on project.  
 
  Next Steps  
While the prototype system tested the main question s of computer vision and bi -manual unfolding, 
there are several key areas that may present issues in a commercial system and will require further 
investigation going forward.  The primary difference between the lab setup and a r eal laundry is the 
environmen tal conditions, including changing lighting and shadows , high  humidity and temperature, 
and static electricity build -up due to so much moving linen. How the system and the towels 
themselves will respond to these circumstances is currently unknown.  
In any c ommercial offering, or even in use at the current clien t’s facility, the system must prove to 
be extremely reliable, and a clear improvement over the existing system. Any errors will be viewed 
harshly, and so these environmental factors, while somewhat tan gential to the core vision 
technologies, will be critic al. Luckily, most of these are relatively straightforward problems in the 
computer vision and industrial control fields, but finding affordable solutions that scale to the whole market will be a long -term project.  
The requirements at each of these future customer’s laundries may be different, with constraints on the available workspace, uptime/maintenance requirements , and different requirements for the 
overall flatness of the towels before they are pas sed on to downstream systems. For example, the 
client in this case has several folding lines available and can ensure by pre -sorting that the system 
would always receive towelling. Smaller laundries may not have this pre -sorting step or spare lines 
to proc ess different products, meaning the system may receive products that are not foldable, so a 
product type detection step would be necessary.  
There are also some development questions about the process generated during the prototyping 
work . For example, while passing the towel from one arm to another, the towel tends to fold over 
itself in a predictable manner, only revealing a corner after a turn. With more experimentation this property might be revealed to be a function of the orientation and relative heigh ts of the grippers . If 
this is the c ase, rather than simply shaking the towels to randomise them, it might be possible to use 
the property to speed up the grabbing process and reduce the randomness.  
Another question raised was whether the corner detection computer vision system could be augm ented by adding in the RGB information that is discarded after training. If the dye used to paint 
the edges for training could be made invisible to the camera, either by matching it with a filter , 
controlling the lightin g setup, or through digital processi ng, then the neural network would have the 
chance to use shadows and hems in its classification.  
To resolve the answers to the above questions  and prepare the technology for commercial 
deployment, a follow -on project is proposed. This project would aim to raise the Technology 
Readiness Level from its current TRL 4  (lab validation of prototype) to TRL 7 ( integrated pilot system 
demonstrated) , deploying a  high -performance  pilot system on site in one of the client’s laundri es. 
The follow -on project would bu ild on the practical and commercial learnings found in this project, 
particularly those around software architecture and control, computer vision architecture, and  
workspace layout.  For example, the Robot Operating System had its benefits  during the 
development process, but ultimately ended up wasting  more development time than it saved , 
exposing many edge cases and stability issues that would be near -impossible to maintain in a 
deplo yed system. On the other hand, Docker co ntainers proved to be a much more solid and 
scalable platform to develop on , with far better automation, isolation , and documentation than ROS . Similarly, the vision system required a  USB3.1  connection  to communicate  with the Realsense 
cameras, which meant  using cables that were only 2m long, constraining camera placement and 
workspace layout. Using USB also presented many reliability issues, as the cameras would 
sometimes fail to enumerate themselves with the worksta tion. Both these issues would be solved in 
a future project by  using industrial- style self- managed  cameras that can be accessed over a reliable 
connection like ethernet.  
Based on these learnings, the team  can more  accurately estimate  and cost -up the skillsets, 
equipment , and engineering effort t hat will be required to develop a pilot system . A preliminary  
estimate of the timeline and budget for such a project is attached as A ppendix  3, while additional 
learnings are attached as Appendix 4 . 
  Conclusi o n 
The aim of the project was to prove out the viability of a computer vision driven, bi -manual towel 
unfolding concept,  and this goal was achieved with great success . The system that was developed 
can fill a critical gap in the automation of commercial laundries  that is currently relies on 
unpredic table labour availability .  
There a re clear pathways for increasing the throughput and accuracy of the system, and no hard 
barriers  to scale  were discovered.  The project utilised generic robotic and vision systems that were 
already on hand  at the ARM Hub a nd showed  a throughput capacity that is comparable to the 
current human process.  A follow -on TRL 7 on-site pilot project  as described above , with hardware 
and vis ion systems specified for the environment , should be able to push the  performance into the 
range where it can more than  handle existing manual  capacity .  
With broad adoption of robotic systems in the laundry industry, the sector can become more 
resilient to economic impacts from tourism an d labour availability  due to COVID -19 or other 
challenges. T his will allow for more confident investment in laundries like CLS  and the industries that 
rely on their se rvices.  
Per CLS’s Tom Roberts, “ The biggest benefit that we have seen is the flow- on effects that this project 
with have going into the future. So, we have started off with towelling items but that can grow  into 
other products that we process every day, such as other textile items, sheets, pillowcases… There’s a lot of applications within the laundry industry itself and probably outside of the laundry  industry 
where this type of technology can be integrated in all sorts of environments .” 
This versatility and scalability of the techniques used in this project is unique in the laundry space, 
and there are plenty of opportunities in industries well beyo nd this sector . The experience gained by 
their impleme ntation will prove extremely valuable when it comes to adapting them  to new domains 
in the future.

1.   Problem description  What is the problem / gap / opportunity that this manufacturing R&D project is 
intending to solve / fill / create?  
Traditional aerial search from unmanned systems requires the pilot to 
supervise the aircraft at the same time as monitoring the video stream to 
identify targets. Besides the distraction of multiple tasks, the video stream is 
often of low quality (due to the bandwidth of the transmission system) and 
displayed on small monitors that are difficult to read in daylight. The current 
solution to this issue is to use multiple operators in dedicated vehicles fitted 
with high bandwidth systems w ith large daylight readable screens. This is an 
expensive exercise which is not financially viable for small voluntary search 
and rescue organisations.  
 
Whilst ADR can supply drones capable of supporting the current approach, 
this does not create a competitive advantage for ADR.  Currently the market 
uses Chinese manufactured drones.   
 
ADR will not be able to compete on price alone.  In line with the successful 
approach used for the underground mining sector, their intention is to provide 
a capability, which in turn enables the manufacture of the core UAS by ADR.

What type of advanced technologies or innovative approaches will be 
adopted or created? What is unique about the project?  
This project involves the adaptation of an existing QUT machine vision 
capability for the new application of autonomously identifying humans from an 
aerial platform. Off -the-shelf machine vision systems only detect people from 
a ground perspective. However  in the Search and Rescue and Emergency 
rescue applications considered for the capability developed in this project, 
people need to be detected from the air, moreover they may be standing, 
sitting, prone or partially occluded by trees.  
The detection will be an active vision process, developed in two stages;  
 
Stage 1  
o First stage aims for a high recall at high altitude (in order to cover a 
large search area quickly and not miss any target). Because of the high 
recall, the precision might be low.  
o This stage will require the collection of data at various heights, in 
various lighting conditions and various terrains to create a data set of 
images of humans in various poses. The combination of these four

variables will require hundreds of hours of flights, The experience of the 
QUT team will then be applied to developing machine learning based 
on low resolution images. This is highly specialised research which will 
benefit from that already completed by QU T in their numerous AI 
projects.  
 
Stage 2  
o The second stage consists of the UAS autonomously defining flight 
paths to enable for alternative angles/perspectives on the target, 
increasing the confidence in the sighting.  
o To achieve this, ADR will develop a number of automated flight 
behaviors or “scripts”. The QUT software, when it detects a probable 
target, will trigger a script such as a spiral descent centered on the 
target location to provide higher and higher resoluti on images while 
avoiding obstacles such as trees. This functionality is not available on 
any of the commercial drones used by the police or fire and rescue 
services.  
 
The unique aspect of this project is the modification of state -of-the-art 
machine vision systems to ADRs UAS, creating an innovative capability 
through this integrated combination.  Combining ADRs and QUTs proven 
capabilities, this targets a relatively rap id solution for a complex problem.

The AIGP program was developed to certify professionals in the field of AI governance. The 
AIGP credential exhibits a fundamental understanding of AI governance and comprehension of 
best practices for responsible management of AI systems in the U.S., EU and other jurisdictions.
Subject matter areas include: 
• Foundations of AI — key terms and definitions, differences among types of AI systems, AI 
use cases, history and evolution of AI.
• AI impacts and principles — identifying risks and harms of ungoverned AI systems, 
characteristics of ethical AI, responsible AI governance, and risk management.
• AI laws and life cycle — how current laws intersect with the use of AI and major 
frameworks, current and emerging global regulations (such as the EU AI Act and Canada’s 
Bill C-27), AI system planning, design, development, implementation, testing and 
maintenance.
• Awareness and accountability — liabilities of AI systems, user concerns, monitoring, 
auditing and adaptation to evolving standards.        AIGP Study Guide  4

The IAPP recommends you prepare in the following manner:
1. Review the body of knowledge  
The body of knowledge for the AIGP program is a comprehensive outline of the subject matter 
areas covered by the AIGP exam. The integrated exam blueprint indicates the minimum and 
maximum number of items included on the AIGP exam from the major areas of the body of 
knowledge. Questions may be asked from any of the topics listed under each area and can be 
used to guide your preparation. Studying the body of knowledge can help you further target  your 
primary study needs and determine which areas merit additional focus in your preparation. 
2. Get certification training
The IAPP offers in-person, live online and self-paced online certification prep classes to help 
you prepare for your exams. You can find a list of scheduled classes or purchase self-paced 
online training in the IAPP store.
3. Review IAPP preparation resources   
Resources for exam preparation are available on the topic page for artificial intelligence on the 
IAPP website, where you can navigate by topic and also view featured resources. Find articles, 
reports, a glossary of terms and networking opportunities with other AI governance professionals.        AIGP Study Guide  5

and standards.

B. Understand the key steps in the AI system design phase.

B. Integrate AI governance principles into the company or institution.

The AIGP is a three-hour exam composed of 100 items. Most of the items are multiple choice, 
including both single stand-alone questions and others associated with AI case studies. Also, 
there are some alternative item types that require the test-taker to move answer options into a 
certain order or categories. There are no essay questions. Each correct answer is worth one point.

© IAPP 2023. All rights reserved.The IAPP Certification Program Structure
The IAPP currently offers four certification programs: the Artificial Intelligence Governance 
Professional (AIGP), the Certified Information Privacy Professional (CIPP), the Certified 
Information Privacy Manager (CIPM) and the Certified Information Privacy Technologist (CIPT).
AIGP certification demonstrates comprehension of AI systems and the ability to deploy AI in 
a manner that abates risk and ensures safety and trust. It confirms an understanding of AI 
ecosystems, identification and mitigation of bias, and the capability to effectively communicate 
best practices for responsible AI management.
CIPP certification demonstrates a mastery of data privacy laws and regulations and how to 
apply them: jurisdictional laws, regulations and enforcement models, plus legal requirements 
for handling and transferring data. Within the CIPP, there are four concentrations: 
 Asian privacy (CIPP/A).
 Canadian privacy (CIPP/C).
 European privacy (CIPP/E).
 U.S. private-sector privacy (CIPP/US).
CIPM certification demonstrates an understanding of implementing privacy requirements 
in day-to-day operations. It confirms the ability to create a company vision, structure a data 
protection team, develop and implement system frameworks, communicate to stakeholders 
and measure performance.
CIPT certification demonstrates an understanding of privacy’s role in technology, including 
building privacy-friendly products, services and systems; deploying emerging technologies while  
respecting consumer privacy; and establishing privacy practices for data security and control. 
There are no concentrations within the AIGP, CIPM or CIPT — they cross all jurisdictions 
and industries.

process es 
The grant opportunity opens  
We publish the grant guidelines on amgc.org.au/projects . 
 
You complete and submit a technology assessment  application  
You complete the application form , address ing all the eligibility and assessment  criteria in order for your 
application to be considered.  
 
We assess  all Stage 1 Technology application s 
At Stage 1, t he Advanced Robotics for Manufacturing ( ARM ) Hub will  review  technology  applications 
against eligibility criteria and notify you if you are not eligible.  
The ARM Hub will  assess eligible application s against the assessment criteria including an overall 
consideration of the technology to be deployed  and compare it to other eligible applications.  
We notify you if your application fails to meet a 50% score against the merit criteria.  
Applications with a 50% or above score are required to undertake a one -on-one consultation with the 
ARM Hub to review technology and workforce adoption  activities  related to  your application . The 
resulting report will be provided to applicants  and AMGC.  
We notify you if the review s fails to meet an acceptable technology  standard .  
Successful applicants will be asked to submit a Stage 2 Commercialisation  application  to AMGC . 
 
We assess all Stage 2 Commercialisation  applications  
AMGC will review the applications against eligibility criteria and notify you if you are not eligible.  
We assess eligible applications in a triage process against the assessment criteria including an overall 
consideration of value with relevant money and compare it to other eligible applications.  
We notify you if your application fails to meet a 50% score against the merit criteria.  
We notify you if the application  fails to meet an acceptable commercial standard . 
 
We make grant recommendations  
We provide advice to AMGC Board  on the merits of each application.  




We advise you of the outcome of your application.  
 
We enter into a project  agreement  
We will enter into a project  agreement with successful applicants. The type of project  agreement is 
based on the nature of the grant and proportional to the risks involved.  
  Delivery of grant  
You undertake the grant activity as set out in your project  agreement. We  manage the grant by working 
with you, monitoring your progress against milestones and making payments.  
 
Evaluation  of AMGC National Robotics Industry Grant Fund  
We evaluate the specific grant activity and AMGC National Robotics Industry Grant Fund  as a whole. 
We base this on information you provide to us and that we collect from various sources.  
 
2. About the AMGC National Robotics Industry Grant  
Fund  
A. Purpose of the Grant  
 
The objectives of the grant are to fund projects through AMGC’s National Robotics Industry Grant 
Fund  that: 
• Grow Australia’s robotics industry  
• Invest in upskilling employees in robotics related applications  
• Increase exports of Australian robotics technology and equipment  
• Implement innovative robotic installations and processes within the Australian 
manufacturing priority sectors that achieve a TRL9 level  
 
The intended outcomes of the grant are:  
• To increase the competitiveness of Australian robotics and robotics integration companies  
and to commercialise Australian IP  in robotics related fields . 
• To increase productivity and Australian jobs. 
• To increase the capability and competitiveness of Australian manufacturers through the 
implementation of new robotics technologies  
 
B. Activity  
 
Project scope and description  
 
The National Robotics Industry Grant Fund will provide grants to Australian companies to 
commercialise new  robotics products and applications.  The Fund is intended  to fund later stage 
commercialisation, not early -stage  research -based  programs. However, projects  are still 
encouraged to include collaboration with research partners.  
 
Grantees will contribute a minimum of 50% of eligible project costs as cash contributions. Grantees  
cannot fund their contribution from other Commonwealth, State, Territory or local government grant  
source, or use in -kind (non -financial) contributions to match Commonwealth funding. Grantees  
must provide evidence of their ability to fund their contribution in their application.  
 
Consortia, partnerships, and other joint venture arrangements will be able to apply, however , 
AMGC  must verify these arrangements are made with Australia -based companies and that joint 
venture arrangements include at least one SME partner.  
 
Australian industry projects funded through the  National Robotics Industry Grant  Fund may  include 
the following activities :  • Collaboration and networking with other businesses to develop a  commercially viable  
product and establish market  potential.  
• Collaborating with research and technology hubs/centres to test idea , share knowledge  
and upskil l workforce . 
• Engaging external professionals to provide commercialisation and market advice, such as  
             identifying market opportunities and developing a market strategy.  
• Creating distribution strategies, such as market entry pathway and identifying domestic 
supply chains . 
• Developing a product for commercialisation using innovative robotics applications  
• Developing a robotics product or service for commercialisation by an Australian company  
• Commercialising Australian IP in robotics related fields  
• Acquiring, constructing, installing and commissioning of new machinery and equipment to 
facilitate  the project  (limited to 50% of grant funding ) 
• Invest in upskilling employees in robotics related applications (minimum of 2 0% of grant 
funding).  
• Research collaboration as it relates to the validation/viability of later stage 
commercialisation  and knowledge sharing , and  
• Approved production and post -production manufacturing activities related to 
commercialisation.  
 
Project outcomes  
 
The intended outcomes of the National Robotics Industry Grant Fund are to increase the capability 
and competitiveness of Australian industry through the implementation of innovative robotics 
technologies; and to increase productivity and jobs in Australian industry. In  undertaking the 
Activity, the Grantee must comply with the requirements of the grant opportunity  guidelines (as in 
force at the time of application).  
 
3. Grant amount  and grant period  
For this grant opportunity $ 150 million  is available in three $50 million rounds from 2023-24 to 
2025-26. 
The grant amount will be up to 50 per cent  of eligible project expenditure (grant percentage) . 
• The minimum grant amount is $ 100,000  
• The maximum grant amount is $ 1,000,000 . 
 
You are responsible for the remaining 50 per cent of eligible project expenditure , plus any ineligible 
expenditure.  Your  contribution must be cash. You  cannot use funding from other Commonwealth 
State, Territory or local government  grants to fund the balance of your project expenditure not 
covered by the grant.  
 
3.1. Project period  
The maximum project  period is 18 months . 
We may approve a  further extension  provided you complete your project  by 30 June 2027. 
 
4. Eligibility criteria  
We cannot consider your application if you do not satisfy all eligibility criteria.  
   4.1. Who is eligible?  
To be eligible you must:  
• Have an Australian Company Number (ACN)  
• Have an Australian Business Number (ABN ) 
• Be non -tax-exempt  
• Be registered for the Goods and Services Tax (GST)  
• and be  an entity incorporated in Australia , including start -ups and a trading corporation , 
where your trading activities  form a sufficiently significant proportion of the corporation’s 
overall activities as to merit it being described as a trading corporation or  are a substantial 
and not merely peripheral activity of the corporation.  
 
4.2. Additional eligibility requirements  
We can only accept applications : 
• From small and medium -sized Australian enterprises (SMEs) with up to 199 employees 
(headcount)  however larger organisations are eligible to apply  and may be accepted due to 
the project’s  sizable impact on Australian industry  
• With a minimum of $200,000  in eligible project expenditure  
• Where your application clearly identifies the level of job creation in Australia expected from 
your project  
• Where your project aligns with one or more of the National Manufacturing Priorities  
• Where you can provide evidence  that you can complete the project and meet the costs of 
the proje ct not covered by grant funding .  
• Where you can provide  evidence of how you will provide your share of project costs 
including using the  accountant declaration  template  which confirms you can fund your 
share of the project costs, including any ineligible expenditure. The accountant declaration 
template  must be used and  is available on  https://www.amgc.org.au/wp -
content/uploads/2021/01/Financial -viabilty -template.pdf  
We cannot waive the eligibility cr iteria under any circumstances.  
4.3. Who is not eligible?  
You are not eligible to apply if you are : 
• An individual  
• A partnership  
• A trust (however, an incorporated  trustee may apply on behalf of a trust)  
• A Commonwealth, State , Territory or local g overnment body (including g overnment 
business enterprises).  
5. What the grant money can be used for 
5.1. Eligible activities  
Definition of robots  
 
Robots (including cobots) are autonomous machines that can move within their physical 
environment and manipulate objects. Robots have four essential characteristics: sensing, 
movement, energy and intelligence. In general we use the word “robotics” to encompass ALL 
robotics -relevant fields such as computer and machine vision, sensors and sensing systems (IoT), 
artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) as well as automation and autonomous 
systems.  
  Eligible activities may include  the development of : 
• Sensing and perception systems , including vision systems  
• Field robotics  
• Novel end effectors  
• Collaborative robotics  
• Medical robotics  
• Autonomous systems  
• Innovative robotic processes and control systems  
• Autonomous mobile robots , including AGV’s and UGV’s  
• Prototype robotic machinery and equipment  
• Robotic data collection devices  
 
Projects should be included in the Governments National Manufacturing priority list:   
• Resources Technology  
• Agriculture  
• Forestry  
• Fisheries  
• Transport  
• Medical Science  
• Renewables and low emission technologies  
• Defence  
 
Skills development in robotic applications is an essential element of the AMGC National Robotics  
Industry Grant Fund , with a minimum of 20% of grant funding to be allocated to this activity. Typical  
training is evidenced  through relevant programs  provided by robotics companies , system 
integrators , technology hubs , and research and teaching institutions . 
5.2. Eligible expenditure  
You can only spend grant funds on eligible expenditure  you have incurred  on an agreed  project  as 
defined in your project  agreement.  
• For guidance  on eligible expenditure, see  appendix A. 
• For guidance  on ineligible expenditure, see appendix B. 
 
We may update the guidance  on eligible and ineligible expenditure from time to time. If your 
application is successful, the version in place when you submitted your application applies to your 
project.  
 
If your application is successful, we may ask you to verify project costs that you provided in your 
application. You may need to provide evidence such as quotes for major costs.  
 
Not all expenditure on your project may be eligible for grant funding. The Program  Delegate (who is 
an AMGC Projects Director  within AMGC  with responsibility for the program) makes the final 
decision on what is  eligible expenditure and may give additional guidance on eligible expenditure if 
required.  
 
To be eligible, expenditure must : 
• Be a direct cost of the project  
• Be incurred by you for required project audit activities.  
  You may elect to commence your project from the date we notify you that your application is 
approved by AMGC Board .  
 
6. The assessment  criteria  
You must  address all assessment criteri a in Stages 1 and 2 of your application s. We will assess 
your application s based on the weighting given to  each criterion . 
The application form s ask questions that relate  to the assessment criteria  published on AMGC 
website . The amount of detail and supporting evidence you provide in your application  should be 
relative to  the project size, complexity and grant  amount requested . You should provide evidence 
to support your answers . The application form displays size limits  for answers . 
We will only consider funding applications that score highly (50% or more)  against all asses sment  
criterion , as these represent best technology value for money . We will then work  with you to verify 
details of your application. We will reject applications that cannot be verified to a technical or 
commercial standard.  
 
7. How to apply  
Before applying you should read and understand these guidelines,  the FAQs, the sample 
application form a nd the sample project agreement published on AMGC website.  
To apply, you must : 
• Complete  the ARM Hub Stage 1 online technology assessment application form  via 
amgc.org.au  
• If successful with your technology assessment by ARM Hub,  you will invited to submit a 
Stage 2 commercialisation application form via amgc.org.au  
• Provide all the  information requested   
• Address all eligibility and assessment  criteria  
• Include all necessary attachments  
You will receive confirmation of receipt of your application when you submit your technology and 
commercialisation application s. You should retain  a copy of your application  for your own records . 
You can view and print a copy of your submitted application on t he portal for your own records.  
You are responsible for making sure your application s are complete and accurate. Giving false or 
misleading information is a serious offence under the Criminal Code Act 1995  (Cth). If we consider 
that you have provided false or misleading information,  we may not progress  your application. If 
you find an error in your application after submitting it , you can contact us at 
applications@amgc.org.au   
You can apply for more than one project under this grant opportunity , however the first project must 
be completed before the second project can be approved .  
If you need  further guidance around the  eligibility of robotics automation manufacturing projects, 
you may contact the AMGC National Projects director  listed on amgc.org.au  (contact us) . If you are 
unable to submit an application online , please contact applications@amgc.org.au   7.1. Attachments to the application  
You must attach supporting documentation to the application in line with the instructions provided 
within the form. You should only attach requested documents. We will not consider information in 
attachments that we do not request.  
7.2. Timing of grant opportunity  
You can only submit an application between the published opening and closing dates. We cannot 
accept late applications.  
Table 1: Expected timing for this grant opportunity   
Activity  Timeframe  
Assessment of technology applications  5 weeks  
Assessment of commercialisation applications  5 weeks  
Approval of outcomes of selection process  3 weeks  
Negotiation of project  agreements  2 weeks  
Notification to unsuccessful applicants  At the time of the grant decisions  
Earliest start date of project   Date of notification that your project is 
approved by AMGC Board  
End date of grant commitment  No later than 30 June 2026 
8. The grant selection process  
Stage 1  
The ARM Hub will deliver Stage 1 of the AMGC National Robotics Industry Grant.    
ARM Hub reviews  application s against the eligibility criteria . Applications that meet a 50% score  
the selection criteria will undertake a Technology Assessment with the ARM Hub . The technology 
Assessment  is an opportunity  invol ving a one -on-one consultation to review technology and 
workforce skills development related to the application. A report will be provided to the applicant 
and AMGC.  
 
Stage 2  
If your technology application is successful  in Stage 1 , you will be invited to submit a Stage 2 
commercialisation application.  
 
We consider your  Stage 2 commercialisation  application on its merits, based on:  
• How well it meets the criteria  
• How it compares to other applications  
• Whether it provides value with relevant money  
• Whether it meets a technology and commercial standard . 
 
When assessing whether  the application represents value with relevant money, we will have regard 
to:  
• The overall objectives of the grant opportunity  
• The evidence identified to demonstrate how your project  contribute s to meeting th ose 
objectives   • The relative value of the grant sought.  
 
We will establish a triage committee comprised of independent industry experts . The committee 
may seek additional advice from independent technical experts.  The committee will assess your 
application against the assessment criteria and compare it  to other eligible applica tions  before 
recommending which projects to fund . 
 
8.1. Who will approve grants?  
 AMGC Board  decides which grants to approve , taking into account the recommendations of the 
Triage committee  and the availability of grant funds.  
 
AMGC ’s decision is final in all matters, including : 
• The grant approval  
• The grant  funding  to be awarded  
• Any conditions attached to the offer of grant funding.  
We cannot review decisions about the merits of your application . AMGC Board  will not approve 
funding if there are insufficient program funds available across relevant financial years for the 
program.  
9. Notification of application outcomes  
We will advise you of the outcome of your application in writing. If you are successful, we advise 
you of any specific conditions attached to the grant . 
You can submit a  new application for the same (or similar) project if there is future  funding 
availability . You should include  new or more information to address the weaknesses that prevented  
your previous application  from being successful . If a new application is substantially the same as a 
previous ineligible or unsuccessful application,  we may refuse  to consider it for assessment . 
10. Successful  grant applications  
10.1.  Project  agreement  
You must enter into a legally binding project  agreement with AMGC . The project  agreement has 
general terms and conditions that cannot be changed. A sample project  agreement is  available on 
AMGC website . 
We must execute a project  agreement with you before we can make any payments. Execute 
means both you and AMGC  have signed the agreement.  
The approval of your grant may have specific conditions determined by  the assessment process or 
other considerations made by AMGC Board . We will identify these in the offer of grant funding.  
If you enter an agreement under AMGC National Robotics Industry Grant Fund , you cannot receive 
other grants for the same activities  from other Commonwealth , State  or Territory  granting 
programs.  
AMGC  may reco ver grant funds if there is a breach of the project  agreement.  
You will have 30 days from the date of a written offer to execute this project  agreement with 
AMGC . During this time, we will work with you to finalise details.  
The offer may lapse if both parties do not sign the project  agreement within this time. Under certain 
circumstances, we may extend this period. We base the approval of your grant on the information  you provide in your application. We will review any required changes to these details to ensure they 
do not impact the project as approved by AMGC Board . 
10.2.  How we pay the grant  
The project  agreement  will state  the: 
▪ Maximum grant amount we will pay  
▪ Proportion  of eligible expenditure covered by the grant  (grant percentage ) 
▪ Any financial contribution provided by you or a third party  
▪ We will make payments according to an agreed schedule set out in the project  agreement. 
Payments are subject to satisfactory progress on the project.  
10.3.  Tax obligations  
Where applicable we will add GST to your grant payment and provide you with a recipient created 
tax invoice. You are required to notify us if your GST registration status changes during the project 
period.  
Grants are assessable income for taxation purposes, unless exempted by a taxation law. We 
recommend you  seek independent professional advice on your taxation obligations  or seek 
assistance from the Australian Taxation Office . We do not  provide advice on tax.  
11. Announcement of grants  
We will publish non -sensitive details of successful projects on AMGC website . We are required to 
do this by the Commonwealth Grants Rules and Guidelines  unless otherwise prohibited by law.  
This information may include : 
• Name of your organisation  
• Title of the project  
• Description of the project and its aims  
• Amount of grant funding awarded  
• Australian Business Number  
• Business location  
• Your organisation’s industry sector.  
12. How we monitor your grant activity  
12.1.  Keeping us informed  
You should let us know if  anything is likely to affect your project or organisation.  
We need to know of any key changes to your organisation or its business activities, particularly if 
they affect your ability to complete your project, carry on business and pay debts due.  
You must also inform us of any changes to your : 
• Name 
• Addresses  
• Nominated contact details  
• Bank account details.

Describe the key technical challenges to determine the feasibility of your idea or 
technology. *  
The main technical challenge is to translate text -based regulations into a form that can be the basis 
for control of autonomous systems. Rather than human in the translation of regulations into fixed 
code, this needs to be accomplished in a flexible manner  so when the regulations are updated, they 
can be autonomously included in the system designs. Existing work from CSIRO will be leveraged to 
accomplish this task. However, assessing its success will not be trivial due to the breadth and depth 
of the regula tions.  
The next technical challenge is to speak/translate to a common language to ensure mutual 
understanding. Operators, regulators and other stakeholders must be able to communicate in a 
correct and timely fashion with each other and the autonomous system. For example, autonomous 
systems operating in the marine environment may be termed “Cyber -Enabled Ships’ [Lloyd’s 
registry], Unmanned Systems (UxS) [US Coast Guard], and remotely operated vehicle ( ROV ) 
[underwater remotely operated vehicle in academia], and so forth.  
An important challenge is how the key requirements of stakeholders can be assimilated into the 
regulatory framework. For example, how cultural, ethical and customary practices can be encoded in 
a manner by which an autonomous system can accommodate their p rinciples.  
It is critical to identify the criteria that will be used to judge how a system conforms to the 
regulations. How these criteria vary across the Lloyd's Register autonomy level needs to be made 
coherent, i.e. Cyber accessibility levels (AL) for autonomous/r emote access  
AL0 No cyber access – no assessment – no descriptive note – included for information only.  
AL1 Manual cyber access – no assessment – no descriptive note – included for information only.  
AL2 Cyber access for autonomous/remote monitoring.  
AL3 Cyber access for autonomous/remote monitoring and control (onboard permission is required, 
onboard override is possible).  
AL4 Cyber access for autonomous/remote monitoring and control (onboard permission is not 
required, onboard override is possible).  
AL5 Cyber access for autonomous/remote monitoring and control (onboard permission is not 
required, onboard override is not possible).  
It is technically challenging to ensure that as the autonomy on -board a platform increases it is still 
capable of being able to be assured. It needs to be determined how as the autonomy increases (or 
decreases) it is possible to simply amend the regulatory  assessment of the craft rather than start the 
assessment again from scratch.  Creating a simulation that is sufficiently comprehensive to assure the operation of an autonomous 
marine vessel is challenging on the number of simulation platforms that could be utilised. It would 
not be feasible to fully develop a system on each platform  such that a subset of tasks need to be 
tested on the most plausible all prior to making a decision on the best/most suitable platform to 
adopt for the simulation.  
Assessing the range of regulations that the vessel must obey at different ALs is challenging. Decisions 
need to be taken on whether a 'driving test' style that samples possible scenarios to measure/ assess 
behaviour or whether exhaustive compliance testing  is required needs to be made.  
Technically assuring the operation of the vessel is difficult but getting vessel operators/owners to 
use the system happily is another part of the project. Implementing good user -focused design is not 
trivial in order to ensure ease and initialisation of u se. Measuring how well both the regulatory and 
operating users of the system interact with it requires social science skills, such as ethics and 
personal data handling. Similarly, new criteria will need to be defined on how well the various types

considered. Further, how the simulation can be combined with/lead on to real -world testing needs

vessel does not meet the regulations: how this is described, why it occurred and what can be 
charged to meet the requirement needs to be conveyed in an action able manner?  
A simulation testing autonomous vessels is capable of producing big data, which introduces a 
technical challenge. How records are kept in a legal, searchable and useful manner needs work. AI
