Papers  
• Towel dragging  
 
Dual Edge Classification  
A paper titled Dual edge classifier for robust cloth unfolding  (Gabas, Kita, & Yoshida, 2021)  shows a 
method for grabbing  the adjacent corners of a held towel corner using computer vision and deep  
learning techniques.  
The most promising aspect of this papers is that i t outlines the use of a RGB and depth camera to 
collect training data of a towel with green painted edges held by a single robot gripper. The edges  of 
the towel are segmented using the RGB data and this is then used as the ground truth to train a 
classifier that uses only depth information. This means that a large amount of training data can be 
automatically generated with the painted towel, without requiring that any towels are painted in the 
final system  since the depth camera does not consider colours.   
 This method of data collection minimises what is traditionally the most labour -intensive element of 
deep learning methods, which means we can take advantage o f the flexibility and power of deep 
learning models without having to invest as much time in development as other options.  
 
Patents  
 
   
 Experimentation  
Validation of Concepts  
The first experiment was designed to test whether the  towel unfolding task could be completed at 
all using the equipment available at the ARM Hub. This involved first determining a simple method 
of achieving the unfolding itself.  
This method relies on the geometry of a towel held by its corner. The point of the towel furthest 
away from the held corner will always be the diagonally opposite corner unless the towel has not 
been completely stretched out.  If this opposite corner is also grabbed, and both held corners are 
lifted off the ground, then gravity will cause the new lowest points of the towel to be the remaining 
two corners.  One of these corners can be grabbed in exchange for one of the held diagonal corners, 
and the two corners will be adjacent. At this point, the two held corners can be lifted and spread 
apart to flatten the towel.  
To determine whether this was possible with a single robotic arm, an experiment was set up  where  
the force of gravity was replaced with tension generated by a fixed tool with  a specific geometry.  
The towel is first grabbed by its corner by the robot and dragged through the tool horizontally , onto 
a flat table . The tool ensures that the towel stays straight throughout  the dragging process and that 
the opposite corner ends up as the furthest point away from the held corner.   
The robot when then let go of the corner it was holding  and a simulated gripper then grabbed that 
same corner to hold it still . The robot then moved  to grab the opposite corner near the tool.  This 
corner was then lifted into the air  and shaken so the towel stretched between it and the simulated 
gripper, emulating stage 2 in the above process. The robot then lay the towel down on the table in 
this triangular shape  and let go . Finally, the robot would grab one of the remaining ungrabbed 
corners and unfold the  towel from triangular to rectangular.  
 
 
  
Validation of Computer Vision Approach  
To ensure that computer vision was a useful method of detecting towel corners , a prototype  
machine learning system was created, following the example found in a paper published by X. This 
prototype  implemented the same architecture as the paper, but less time was spent tuning and 
collecting data. The end result was a usable corner detecting computer vision system, that had 
somewhat lower accuracy than the paper , but has plenty of room for tuning in the future . 
The machine learning architecture combines  the outputs of  two deep learned neural network 
classifiers operating in two different modes . Both  classifiers  take a depth image of a towel and 
produce a pixel -wise prediction of where the “real” edges of the towel a re in the frame. The “real” 
edges are defined in contrast to the “non -real” edges of the towel in the image , which are the lines 
on the towel caused by folds or creases  rather than the physical edge .  
The type of edge is important when it comes to classifying the type of corners  visible in the image. 
When a towel is hanging from a single corner, the lowest point on the towel in the image will likely 
be the opposite corner, with the two adjacent corners somewhere higher up. The left and rightmost 
extremes of the towel in the image are promising places to look for corners , so these two points are 
then considered by a corner classification algorithm outlined in the paper.  
The types of the edges leading to a particular corner can be  used to determine if the corner is “real”, 
as in, an adjacent corner to the one being held,  a corner folded forward or backwards , or 
unclassifiable.  If the corner is a real one, a command can be sent to a robot arm to grab it , but if the 
corner is folded forward or backward, then the arm holding the towel can be commanded to rotate 
the towel so that the corner is more visible and easier to grab.  
Validation of Dual Robot Control Framework  
   
 Client Consultation  
Given the above research, the ARM Hub staff determined that there were several viable paths 
forward and decided to consult with the client about which would be of most utility to their 
business. The approaches discussed and the goals they were designed to meet are listed below. The 
client ultimately decided it would be best for the ARM Hub team to focus on throughput, maximizing 
the technology level in the approach, with further commercialization to occur at a later time.  
Goals  
• As thoroughly developed a product as possible by the end of the project  
• Minimise unit cost  
• Maxmise throughput  
• Minimise error rate  
• Minimise footprint/maximise portability  
• Maximise ease -of-use  
• Maximise range of acceptable towels  
 
Focus on Developing Most Promising Method  
This approach would involve using a single robotic arm that implements the already demonstrated 
unfolding algorithm. This involves finding and grabbing a towel by its corner straight out of the bin, 
then dragging it across a table to unfold the towel. Requ ires the assistance of one or two 
supplementary grippers to aid in stretching out the towel.  
The focus of the project would be on maximising the reliability and improving the packaging of the 
setup, aiming to produce a self -contained, readily -deployable product.  
Advantages  
• Method is relatively proven and likely to result in a deployable product for the client  
• Uses only equipment that we already have  
• Easily replicable  
• Ease -of-use work (e.g.  user interface) could be re -used for future process improvements   
Disadvantages  
• Opportunity cost. A better solution might be out there  
• Mediocre speed. May require multiple systems to achieve desired throughput  
• High unit cost floor due to collaborative robot  
• Large footprint. Needs a table  
  
Focus on Throughput  
This approach would use as many arms as necessary to minimise the cycle time of a single 
installation. It would likely involve an arm lifting a towel from any location based on a simple depth 
image algorithm, with a second arm grabbing the lowest corner, t hen the first arm grabbing an 
adjacent corner based on a machine learning algorithm. This leaves the pair of arms with an 
unfolded towel ready for placement.  
The focus of this project would be about finding the highest performing possible combination of 
existing technologies in order to help prove the system to the market, with optimisations and 
reliability increases coming later.   
 Advantages  
• Would serve as a great demo for clients and investors  
• Relatively known technologies  
• Highest technology option. Produces more research that could be commercialised  
• High throughput for the footprint  
Disadvantages  
• Very high unit cost floor due to multiple collaborative robots  
• Risky due to high technology ambition  
• Less focus on a deployable end product  
  
Focus on Cost  
This approach would immediately start work on a novel design not based on an expensive high -
degree -of-freedom robotic arm. This would involve designing a robotic system with minimal 
degrees -of-freedom, cost -effective actuators, and advanced computer vision  algorithms to replace 
mechanical methods.  
The focus on this project would be to determine the minimum cost for a system that can perform 
the job, de -risking the ROI calculations for the client and potential investors. The project would 
involve much more risk due to the chance of novel systems not performing as expected.  
Advantages  
• Would demonstrate a unit cost floor for mass deployment, assisting with ROI 
calculations  
• May be necessary work in the future regardless of chosen option  
• Custom robot would make for a unique, industrial demo  
• Low unit cost  
Disadvantages  
• Risky due to custom robotics and advanced computer vision  
• Less focus on a deployable end product  
• Probable large footprint  
• Likely slower than other solutions

2.1 Root Suppression  Context   
Tree root invasion is a primary contributor to sewer pipe blockages and asset damage, which costs

Urban Utilities currently use a range of technologies to remove tree roots obstructing sewer pipes.

customer -specific item, adopting off- the-shelf automation solutions in their load pin

1. Load Pin Strain Gauge Installation  
Installing strain gauges in load pins requires two sub -processes: load pin registration and holding, 
and strain gauge insertion. The load pin needs to be fixtured in a manner that allows for both the 
consistent and concentric insertion of gauges, and the d etection and correction of the load pin’s 
orientation for correct gauge placement.  
 
The proposed solution would utilise a stationary chuck to hold the load pin from the bottom end, 
ensuring the engraved head cap was still exposed. On the other end, there would a vision system 
for registering the pin’s orientation. This system would look for the arrow engraved on the cap to 
determine its orientation. After this, either the chuck holding the pin, or the strain gauge insertion 
mechanism would rotate accordingly to ensure the gauges are placed at the correct positions.

Further detail about the strain gauge mechanism process has been previously discussed.  
This project could be extended to include a machine tending robot that does the loading and

2. Bar or Gantry Loading and Unloading for CNC Lathes  
This proposal involves the integration and adaption of off the shelf automation equipment to 
increase automation capacity in the machining areas. These would help free up current staff and 
resources to focus on other priorities.  
 
Each system has trade -offs; a bar loader or gantry machine tender would feed stock into the 
lathes, allowing large, automated batch runs but would have limited part handling options. A gantry system has more ha ndling options but requires the stock to be cut to length ahead of time.  
We would involve a local robotic integrator who would do the adaption and servicing of either of 
these machines. Pending further discussions, we would engage with them for further quo ting.  
 
3. Robotic Sandblasting, or Magnetic Deburring  
Currently, all Delphi load pins are sandblasted manually by a machinist after heat treating. This is 
completed to improve the aesthetics of their product. This is the step that is usually skipped under 
time-pressure in larger production runs.   
 The operator currently sandblasts the entirety of the load pin for ease. However, only the pin 
waists and end flanges are required to be finished since the remainder of the pin is later post -
machined.  
 
This finishing operation is a bottleneck for Delphi as it requires time from the expert machinist. 
The priority, implied by previous discussions, in automating this process is to reduce labour time.  
One possible solution would be a robotic arm that utilis ed a similar workpiece holder to the one 
described in the strain gauge installation section. A method to load and unload the pin into the 
holder would need further investigation, but it is likely the throughput would not change. We 
would also involve an in tegrator for this process.

The two key grants focussed on  here are Innovation Connections and IMCRC Activate grants.  
 
1. Innovation Connections  
This is a two -step process that “assists businesses to understand their research needs, connect 
with the research sector and fund collaborative research projects.” This ent ire grant comes at no 
cost to a business. Assuming eligibility (criteria here ), the first step of the grant provides a 
facilitation service and a highly skilled person who will work with the business to uncover strategic 
research needs and opportunities, resulting in a Service Report. The second phase allows the business to undertake a research project that addresses recommendations made in  the Service 
Report. Through a collaboration with a Publicly Funded Research Organisation (PFRO), the 
business can decide on either a researcher placement (which brings a PFRO researcher into the 
business), business researcher placement (which places a res earcher from the business into a 
PFRO), or a graduate placement (which brings a non -PFRO affiliated graduate or post -graduate 
into the business).  
 
ARM Hub can assist with the application process and have had success with previous applications. 
An Innovation Connections grant is a stepping- stone for a company to learn and engage in 
research and typically leads to much larger research grants in the fut ure.  
 
2. Metal 3D Printing of Load Pins  
Traditional manufacturing processes typically do not allow for customisation of products to 
happen easily. Utilising digital fabrication methods such as 3D printing gives users access to tools 
and processes that make it much easier to prototype and manufacture bespoke products. 3D 
printing would be able to take advantage of the strong 3D modelling skillset Delphi already 
exhibits and promotes flexibility in design at no extra cost.  
 There is potential for expanding De lphi’s product range with this manufacturing capability and 
presents a strong research case to see whether 3D printing in metal would be viable for load pins.  
Markforged and Aurora Labs are two examples of suppliers of metal 3D printers with local 
operati ons. Each provides a specification for their printable materials but a key factor to consider 
is the actual printing process. Markforged uses a multi -step process: print, solvent bath, then 
sinter, and this is likely to induce some inconsistency between pr ints. Whereas Aurora Labs’ 
process may produce stronger and more homogenous parts by using direct metal laser melting 
that deposits and melts a thin layer of powder simultaneously.  
 
There are lots of possibilities here and the concept could be a project that is further investigated 
through an Innovation Connections gra nt.

Laser welding  
Challenges  
Traditional robots used for welding are typically precise enough for laser welding but not accurate 
enough when welding butt joints.  
This can be overcome in a few ways:  
1. Restricting the degrees of freedom in the robot to generally increas e the accuracy.  
2. Explore the use of stationary mirror actuated laser welding.  
3. Resolving the accuracy issue with additional sensors . 
4. Or design for a different weld . 
Identify the approach with the best ROI  
We have identified four paths forward within robotic laser welding.  
1. Welding of lower precision parts  ±1mm  
Implement a 6 DOF robot arm , laser welding unit  and potential rotator . Welds of this accuracy can 
be achieved by design overlap into parts. An example part could be the SUV battery cooling system 
shown to ARM Hub.  Pros  
• Lower  barrier to entry.  
• High degree of freedom increases  the versatility of welding cell  
• Starts the pipeline to more accurate generic part welding.  
Cons  
• Limited to lower precision parts.  
2. Implement SCARA style 3 DOF robot arm for laser welding  
Implement robotic laser welding using a SCARA robot. The lower degree s of freedom reduces  the 
accumulated inaccuracy  and if required a platform can be brought in from medical robotics.  This 
platform could also be coupled with a rotator table.  
Pro 
• Increased accuracy of welding down to ±0.1mm  
Cons  
• Decreased versatility of the robotic welder  
• Suitable products to be identified  
3. Stationary laser welding with actuated mirror  
Implement a mirror -actuated  laser welding unit . This style of unit typically has greater accuracy than 
robot -mounted units . With such units, care needs to be taken to align the parts.  
Pro 
• Increased accuracy of welding down to ±0.1mm  
Cons  
• Decreased versatility of the robotic welder  
• Suitable products to be identified  
4. Welding of high precision parts ±0.1mm  
Implement a 6 DOF robot arm, laser welding unit, additional high accuracy sensor  and potential 
rotator. The addition of a n external sensor would allow the robotic arm to adapt for accumulated  
inaccuracies in the robot arm.  
Pro 
• Increased accuracy of welding down to ±0.1mm  
• Can be an extension of the implementation of option 1  
Cons  
• High level of system sophistication  required.  
• No local examples known.  
Recommendations  
ARM Hubs recommended approach to robotic laser welding is to implement option 1 Welding of 
lower precision parts  with a planned path to option 4 w elding of high precision parts . This approach 
provides a fast path to robotic welding functionality while working towards  more general capability 
within PWR’s manufacturing processes.  Develop specifications for procurement.

Lessons Learned implementing LLMs in Australian SME Manufacturing  
 
Australian small to medium sized enterprise (SME) manufactur ers have  a productivity 
challenge: the resources  invested by companies are not returning high enough profit 
margins to spur further  growth (source) . Rapid advancement s in, and the ubiquitous uptake 
and development of Generative AI platforms like ChatGTP, and particularly  the use of  Large 
Language Models (LLMs)  that underpin many of them, can be an immediate part of 
remedying these low productivity levels . Among SMEs, it is not necessarily the expense of 
adopting new technologies that is the barrier – or it certainly isn’t the only barrier - it is trust 
that AI will work as intended  and being able to access the talent to make it  happe n without 
facing perilous consequences for the business (source). This chapter shares our lessons 
learned on implementing  LLMs in Australian SME manufactur ing. We will describe  the 
services in demand by SME manufacturers and outline the decisions that software architects 
are making to achieve the DevOp s goals  of these services .  
 
Why is Australian SME manufacturing important? Nation states around the world are in a 
race to secure their place in high -value global manufacturing supply chains. Evident to 
governments and policy makers before COVID -19, was the fact that countries with a strong 
medium -sized manufacturing sector were successfully  commercialising science and 
technology innovation s and were performing as vital engine rooms for the wider economy 
as they scaled businesses, built robust supply chains and created high value jobs  (source) . 
Countries without a strong manufacturing capability, like Australia, were conversing seeing 
their investment in R&D and innovation taken offshore to be commercialised and were 
suffering the effects of a hollowed -out SME economy and talent drain  (IISA 2023) .  
 
The lack of ventilators and Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) during COVID -19, the 
geopolitical instability that dismantled global supply chains during  the Ukraine war , and the 
looming threat of economic recession have all heavily impacted Australia and r evealed just 
how fragile our manufacturing sector and its supply chains are. Since these occurrences,  the 
nation’s ability to make things has become a topic of widespread public debate  from kitchen 
tables to cabinet rooms. Manufacturing is now deemed not just essential  for the economy 
and jobs; it is a critical  sovereign cap ability to be invested in for its inherent benefits.  
 
Government is implementing new  policy measures to build the Australia’s  sovereign 
manufacturing capability , including m easures that seek to  close the loop on commercialising 
the nation’s research locally (source) and to ‘crowd -in’ private investment  in manufacturing 
with matched government funds (source) . But implementing artificial intelligence in 
manufacturing, particularly  GenAI , will require a new approach from Australia’s innovation 
ecosystem. The commercialisation of GenAI solutions into our SME manuf acturers will come 
from commercial providers or intermediaries between commercial and research providers, 
and will not follow a university lab IP creation to market commercialisation path. This is 
particularly clear given GenAI is an invention  from  big tech business  and requires a 
commercial mindset and resourcing to succeed. Australian manufacturing needs the support 
of the AI ecosystem  including DevOps capability , to keep up with its global competitors that 
will be rapidly incorporating GenAI  into their businesses  and business models, and we can 
address uniquely Australian challenges  like manufacturers of AI enabled drones for bushfire 
management or onsite high -value component manufacturing for remote mining sites that could also be source of unique comparative and competitive advantage for Australian AI 
companies  globally.

1.2 Desktop study (literature review) of existing banana de -
handing  technology  
As early as 1985, Franklin identified the mechanisation  of banana de -handing as a means to improve banana 
processing in packing sheds [1].  To better understand why such devices are not commonly found  in banana 
packing sheds, it is vital to understand current practices.  In February 2022, we undertook a time and motion 
study as described in section 2.7 in conjunction with a desktop study of de -handing automation attempts 
documented to date. Banana harve sting, de -handing and packing are still largely manual, repetitive and labour -
intensive processes [2].  The de -handing process occurs once  banana bunches have been transported to the 
packing shed, had their protective covers removed, and have entered the packing shed.  The quality of the cut 
during the de -handing process influences the subsequent grade given to the banana hand [3].  Once  bananas 
are de -handed, the stalk is discarded, and the bananas are sorted into clusters, washed and packed.  Banana de -
handing is a repetitive and labour -intensive task completed at a core integration point in banana processing  
between the field and the packing shed, making de -handing a prime candidate for automation and robotics. It 
is anticipated that automating the de -handing process would decrease manual labour and offer the potential to 
add value to downstream processes such  as grading and sort ing. 
Previous studies in improving the banana de -handing process identified risks of repetitive strain injury to 
workers’ wrists and hands [4].  As a result of these studies, approaches were recommended to minimise the risk 
to de -handers from all injury types.  For example, to reduce de -handers cutting themselves, it was recommended 
that de -handers use mesh gloves on the hand supporting the bana na bunch and mechanical de -handers were 
also explored. Other recommendations included improving packing sheds to allow an adequate workspace to 
prevent de -handers from cutting other operators and reduce repetitive strain injuries through job rotation and 
worker training initiatives.  
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
A motion study looking to quantify the repetitive strain injuries suffered by banana de -handers identified 
significant strain on workers spines and hips in addition to their wrists and hands [5].  The motion study further 
identified the type of knife as playing a role in the injuries suffered.  The knives used by banana de -handers 
varied between standard knives, curved knives and a unique  spatula style knife.  While completing the motion 
study detailed in [5], all banana de -handers used curved knives developed explicitly for banana de -handing [6].  
The spatula style knives ( Figure 3) comprise a semicircle blade at the end of an extensive handle designed to 
keep the workers' hand clear of the stalk when de -handing bananas.  The semicircle blade of the spatula style 
knives, like the knife described in the patent [7], fits the radius of the banana stalk allowing the de -hander to 
push the knife down to remove the banana hands.  The development of various task -specific knives  Has 
ultimately sought to reduce strain on workers’ hands, wrists, spine and hips. Meanwhile, banana de -handing has 
remained essentially a manual task.  
The earliest attempt identified in the literature to mechanically de -hand bananas literature was a set of spinning 
blades suspended above a tank of water designed and built -in 1985.  After removing the bell, dummy hands and 
shaping the stalk, the de -hander  would lower the bunch into the spinning blades.  While lowering the bunch of 
bananas, the operator could vary the distance between the blades to match the stalk diameter by controlling 
the rotation speed of the device.  The separated hands would fall onto  a rotating foam pad before landing in a 
water bath for washing.  Familiar with the device, Stewart Lindsay Team Leader - Banana Production Systems 
with Department of Agriculture and Fisheries, recalls damage to the fruit was one significant hurdle to 
wide spread implementation of such a device.  Beyond damaging the fruit, the quality of the cut when removing 
banana hands from the bunch affected the grade and subsequent price of the fruit [3]. Because of this quality 
control issue and the significant post -harvesting value of the banana crop [8], much of the existing literature 
focuses on the cutting mechanism of mechanical de -handing.  Figure 3: Spatula style knives 
aim to keep the user’s hands 
clear of the stalk [7].  
 Figure 4: Curved knives 
specifically developed for 
banana de -handing [6].  
 
 
 
Mechanical de -handing splits into two categories, static blade and rotary cutting.  Static blade de -handers utilise 
gravity or pressure from above to feed the stalk of the banana bunch through an adaptive blade or set of combs 
which remove the banana hands  as the stalk progresses.  In contrast to passive blades, the rotary cutting de -
handers use a motor to drive a circular blade down along the stalk to remove the bananas from the bunch.  It is 
important to remember that cut quality needs to be high for eith er approach when separating the hands from 
the bunch.   
Static blade de -handing works by suspending a bunch of bananas above a de -handing mechanism and lowering 
or pushing the bunch. As the bunch lowers, the hands of bananas are removed from the stalk.  While the method 
of de -handing the bananas is similar, the  design of the cutting edge and how it adapts to the changing diameter 
of the banana stalk varies between approaches.  The Ielis patent [9] describes  an adaptable diameter circular 
blade that expands and contracts to suit the stalk. As can be seen in the p atent drawings provided ( figure 5 ), 
four quarter -circle blades slotted into the neighboring  blade while a sprung linkage maintains contact with the 
banana stalk . 
The patent by Zhou [10] describes a set of five comb style blades connected via a pivoting linkage ( figure 4 ).  
Each comb attaches to the pivoting joint with a spring allowing adaption to the stalk's diameter.  Work to 
optimise the comb style banana de -handers ( figure 5 )[11] explored many variables in the mechanism, including 
the number, size and shape of combs, the size of the thin cutting linkages and the speed at which the cutting 
was performed [3].  The banana de -handing device described in [11] and subsequent patent application [12] 
described a seven -bar linkage combed blade ring.  The ring, capable of expanding to a diameter of 164mm and 
compressing to 43mm, comprises six combs and a constant force component ( figure 6 ). As the combs removed 
the hands, the constant force component maintains the mechanism's contact with the banana stalk. Work 
described by Duan in patent [13] decreases the effort and time to de -hand a bunch of bananas.  The mechanism 
consists of three pairs of combs linked with two cutting links that create the circular cutting ring.  The mechanism 
is mounted on top of a movable work surface. The worksurface c an raise and drop, and by raising the mechanism 
and banana bunch the dropping action forced the bunch through the cutting combs.   Static blade de -handers 
used pressure from above or gravity to push the bananas through a series of cutting combs and links t o remove 
the banana hands from the bunches.  Application of these devices showed them to be functional and create 
clean cuts when removing the hands.

The rotary cutting de -handers use a circular rotating blade, as the name suggests.  The stalk passes through the 
blade's center .  The review found two approaches: a handheld device lowered over the bunch and a static device 
with the bananas lowered through it.  The device created by Shravan and seen in the video [14] shows a 
handheld rotary banana de -hander.  The prototype device is lowered over the banana stalk removing the banana 
hands.  The demonstrated device is cumbersome and inadvertently removes individual bananas from the hands, 
a non -desirable trait.  The pat ented rotary type banana combing machine  described in [15] shows a similar motor 
configuration driving a pully to spin a cutting edge.

The rotary type  of banana combing machine spins a pair of knives that can vary in their distance to adapt to the 
diameter of the banana bunch stalk.  This de -handing device is mounted on a workbench and is fed from the 
top. As described in Zhou’s patent  [16], The ability to vary the diameter of the cutter is an essential part of 
maintaining the quality of the cut when removing banana hands.   The variable -diameter self -adaptive rotary 
banana bunch cutter consists of  eighteen comb -style blades ( figure 10 ).  The diameter between the blades is 
variable to ensure clean cuts when removing banana hands from bunches. Rotary cutting banana de -handing 
mechanisms spin the blades used to cut the banana hands from the bunch.  One de -handing device that did not 
fall into th e fixed blade  or rotary cutting types was the fretsaw banana de -hander ( figure 8 ) [17].  The fretsaw 
banana de -hander uses a fretsaw and clamp to hold the banana bunches and remove the hands.  The clamp 
positioned below the saw holds the bunch in place by grasping the stalk when the saw is engaged to remove the 
hand.   
The findings of the literature review suggest that a successful banana de -handing automation solution will need 
to adapt to the tapering diameter of banana stalks to achieve the clean -cut produced by current manual banana 
de-handing practices. Paired with banana de -handing are also mechanisms for holding or grasping banana 
bunches.  The farms observed in this current study used a chain looped back on itself that pulled tight under 
gravity to hang the bananas.  This review found two patents for c lamping devi ces from the South China 
Agricultural University (SCAU).  The first such device [18] is a reversible self -locking clamp ( From Left, Figure 10) 
using a pair of screws to actuate the mechanism.  The second patent describes a similar self -locking device with 
an over center  latch (  Figure 11: Over -centre self -locking clamp [18]. ) to actuate the clamp [18].  
Similarly, the work in [20] explores automatic pneumatic clamping and detaching of the banana stem.

The automation of banana de -handing could add value beyond the task of banana de -handing and offers a key 
integration point for adding value to production through improvements in processes prior to and post hand 
removal.  Industry -led attempts at banana ha rvesting automation have seen existing farm equipment such as 
excavators retrofitted with robotic  
banana pickers ( figure 11 ) [20].  The inventor  claimed  such devices decreased  labour costs while noting 
limitations to widespread adaptation, including reluctance to restructure paddocks or change planting practices.  
Further to farm led innovation, there is work exploring banana plant -specific robots and grippers [22].  Yang 
states that specialist grippers for bananas increase safety margins and decrease damage to fruit.  At the same 
time, Zhang proposes a three (3) degree of freedom (DOF) robot arm ( Figure  12: Proposed 3DOF banana 
harvesting robot [22]. ) for banana harvesting [23].  Robotic banana pickers and specialist banana stem 
grippers could be integrated with existing processes as bananas are harvested and enter the packing she  
Despite developments in the use of computer vision for assessing quality to support grading and sorting in 
related applications/crops, the literature review found limited investigation of the use of computer vision to 
support automation in banana de -handin g.  Computer vision has been used for the detection of bananas in the 
paddock as necessary for banana harvesting robots [24].  This ability to segment the hands of bananas using 
colour and texture -based features could be adapted for use in the de -handing processes and value add in the 
sorting and grading of bananas.  Multiple approaches exist to identify banana stalks in the paddock for robotic 
gripper grasping.  M. Chen proposes using stereo cameras to identify the banana stalk and generate a 3D m odel 
(Left, Figure 14: Input and output images for a stereo vision approach to banana stalk 
identification [24]. Left, Figure 14: Input and output images for a stereo vision approach 
to banana stalk identification [24]. ) [25].  
Figure 13: Banana de -hander attachment for and excavator [20]. Figure  12: Proposed 3DOF 
banana harvesting robot [22].   While T. Chen has developed a deep neural network to identify banana bunch stalks [26].  Literature exploring 
computer vision in banana harvesting has demonstrated an ability to segment banana bunches and stalks in the 
paddock.  These existing approaches could be adapted for banana grasping and de-handing and offer the 
opportunity to add value to the process in the packing shed.   
Banana de -handing remains a repetitive, labour -intensive process that can pose a risk to worker safety.  The 
removal of banana hands from bunches upon arrival to the packing shed has been identified as a bottleneck in 
the processing of bananas. This review  looked at existing literature and patents regarding  banana de -handing.  
The literature identifies two mechanical banana de -handing approaches: static blade de -handing and rotary 
cutting de -handing.  The static blade de -hands the bunch utilising gravity or  pressure from above to push the 
banana bunches through a set of variable diameter cutting combs and links.  
Conversely, rotary cutting de -handers use a circular rotating blade, with examples seen of handheld and bench -
mounted equipment.  Both approaches look extensively at adaptable diameter cutting tools to maintain clean 
cuts when removing the banana hand from  the stems.   
This initial desktop study has found that no commercial -ready automation solution has been identified. Cleanly  
removing banana hands from their stalks at a consistent rate will be vital to automating banana de -handing. A 
future solution must address the damage to fruit that has impeded earlier mechanical banana de -handing 
attempts.  Research into banana harvesting robots, and computer vision already in development, offer potential 
new avenues for the development of an effective banana de -handing solutions.

Overview and Growth Opportunities  
 
Mainetec provides a range of high -quality services, for mining and related industries, 
including rebuilds, parts, fabrication and repair. This includes dragline buckets, walkways, 
chutes, stairs, wear liners, excavator buckets, booms, stick and side frames  and PTAW 
(Plasma Transfer Arc Welding). Machinery is large scal e – including a 49m3 excavator 
bucket which they see once per year.  
 
Mainetec experiences high variability and volume of jobs, with no single , repetitive task  
requirement.  Parts are assessed for repair a fter they arrive in the facility. A condition 
monitoring application developed by Mainetec  supports their assessment of wear and 
maintenance requirements. It is understood that the app shows a heat map for high wear 
areas.  Meshing of the 3D scans currently poses challenge s. The workshop uses Solidworks 
for drafting.  
A typical custom rebuild cycle for a mining bucket is 16 to 20 weeks  and costs around $900k . 
This includes stripping down, adding new parts etc. Excavator buckets can be re -built up to 
8x times before they are decommissioned. Rope shovel buckets  can be re -built 10x times 
before replacing. Buckets can be up to 900 tonne.  
 
Some of the machinery can be 10 -years old, having already had eight to ten prior rebuilds. At 
that stage , major components start to be replaced. Over time, this work has led Mainetec to 
develop new products such as the bracket which was designed to move more efficiently 
achieving less wear on the machine. These designs give Mainetec a further competitive edge 
in the market.  A further design development over time has been linerless buckets . 
 
Mainetec acutely feels the shortage of skilled staff in the region and plays a role in 
develop ing the next generation of technicians  with a sustained apprenticeship program that 
hires four apprentice boilermakers each year.   
Mainetec’s leadership considers d igital transformation to be crucial for the business.  
The demand for local sustainment of heavy machinery is growing due to supply chain issues 
and Mainetec is well placed to benefit from this demand . Recent ly Mainetec has entered into 
a longer term contract with major mining compan y, Rio Tinto,  and this creates a further 
opportunity to partner in different ways to invest in the improve ment of  sustainment 
approaches  and return on investment for both Mainetec and the mining partner . 
 
Technology Chall enges/Opportunities  
An investigation of ways to reduce maintenance downtime in mining shovels could lead to a 
significant competitive advantage for Mainetec. The current practice for shovel front end 
assembly repair is based on mining company experience and history . There are 
standardised s ervice cycles in the industry. However in practice,  predictive maintenance is 
based on current wear.  
Working with major partner, Rio Tinto, there are six sites , with three broad categories of iron 
ore (waste, low grade and high grade) . However , there is significant variability in material and 
how aggressive each site is in terms of bucket wear and tear. Measurements of material 
thickness, hours and volume of material moved are used to support predictive maintenance.  
Ultimately, technical solutions would inform Mainetec’s ability to prefabricate buckets and/or 
bucket repairs to reduce the lead time of refurbishments for their clients.  
Goal is to reduce throughput time from12 to 4 -6 weeks through pre -fabrication.  
Opportunity one: Predictive maintenance  through real time data collection  
There is an opportunity to investigate methods of real time detection and measurement 
(sensing) of wear to more accurately predict failure , better prepare for sustainment (reducing 
throughput time)  and reduce overall equipment down time.   
Further, if level of wear and likely requirements of repair were known prior to receiving, there 
would be an opportunity to secure parts/materials and/or pre-fabricate, saving significant time 
and workshop space and increasing throughput.   
Mainetec ha s representatives located at various mining sites which could be engaged to 
undertake scans on site. The challenges include limited connectivity to internet, controlled 
sites (e.g., BHP owns the site), and data management to process the information. Google 
glasses are already in -use by the company . However the ir use is affected by poor reception 
on site.  
 
A range of technologies may be relevant , depending on what the maintenance teams need to 
know . For example, m easurements like vibration magnitude over time, which might imply 
accelerating wear, can be taken by logging sensors attached t o buckets . Other technologies 
like thickness checking with laser or photogrammetry techniques could be useful . Drone 
mounted technology has been developed by CSIRO and is commercially available that 
enables detailed scanning. The approach varies greatly in complexity and cost  depending on 
how much of the bucket needs to be scanned.  
If not already available , one way forward would be to undertake a feasibility study of existing 
and emerging technology. This would be developed based on initial review of data held 
regarding maintenance issues and variables as well as interv iews with stakeholders  – to 
technically define the problem/challenge . The outcome of such a study would be 
identification of the most feasible technologies that could be pursued , including availability 
and development requirements.  
ARM Hub can also assist to develop technical specifications and to determine whether and 
how these technologies could be applied in a cost -effective way over a diverse fleet/sites .  Opportunity two: Data collection in workshop  
To assist their maintenance workshop, Mainetec are interested in scanning technologies that 
can quickly produce accurate 3D measurements of buckets. This would allow drafters to 
generate plans and order materials for replacement parts quickly, reducing the  time taken to 
get the bucket back on -site.  
Such scanning systems could also be used to track wear between services, allowing 
Mainetec to perform predictive maintenance on parts that are wearing faster than expected 
at a given site. Data about these quick -wearing parts could be used to inform future  designs. 
Both these applications could be enhanced by combining in -workshop scanning with real -
time data collection systems collected by Mainetec at the client’s sites.  
There are several technologies in this space that could be suitable, the most powerful of 
which would be fused laser and accelerometer systems like CSIRO’s Wildcat, where a 
sensor can be walked or flown around a target bucket to produce millimetre accurate  models. 
These models could then be compared with the original CAD models of the buckets using a 
process called registration, and any defects or wear patterns could be highlighted.  
Laser systems like Wildcat and photogrammetry, the other major scanning technology, can 
both be disrupted by certain materials and lighting conditions, so some testing will have to be 
performed if these conditions cannot be controlled by Mainetec’s worksho p. 
ARM Hub could help select, evaluate, and customise these technologies for Maintec’s 
needs, bringing along research and development assistance if off -the-shelf products can’t 
achieve what is needed . 
Opportunity three: Automated welding  
Mainetec  currently uses PTAW welding to hardface its ground engagement tools. PTAW 
allows the use of powdered filler materials that are often harder and cheaper than wire -drawn 
filler. The disadvantages of PTAW are that it can be difficult to use in arbitrary orie ntations 
and is most effective in the flat (1G/1F) position. This means that complex parts must first be 
disassembled so they can be effectively welded, increasing maintenance time.  
There has been research into supporting PTAW welding in more complicated positions, 
which could allow for hardfacing on assembled parts, saving disassembly time. The 
downside is that controlling the weld process would likely require the use of a high degre e-of-
freedom robotic arm to ensure consistency.  
As this is not a solved problem but has high potential to deliver a solution that would be world 
leading, it is the  sort of problem  that would best be addressed through a research project 
using ARM Hub robotics resources and research partners.  This could be scoped as a 
commercial research project and/or grant funding could be sought to offset some of the R&D 
costs.  
Opportunity four: Data management  
Mainetec uses Solidworks as their primary CAD package and has a library of over 3500 
models. Some of these models are over 1000MB in size, and the cloud storage solution 
Mainetec is using is reportedly slow and clunky.  A common solution here is to use virtualisation, a service offered by many IT specialists 
where a company runs all user machines as virtual desktops, with the actual software, data, 
and specialised workstations living in a server rack somewhere. This allows many users to 
share the same high -end hardware fr om their low -power personal machines and never need 
to transfer any models over the internet.  
ARM Hub could help research potential suppliers of virtualisation technology and supply 
them with a specification for Main etec’s use case.  
Option 5: Grant support:  
Mainetec  could be well positioned to leverage grant support.  
ARM Hub can support by review ing and provid ing input to automation equipment 
spec ification s as well as provide feedback to strengthen application  and the case for 
advanced manufacturing funding.

Banana De -handing Robot – Preliminary Project Plan  
 
Scope  
This project aims to produce a prototype robotic banana de -handing system at TRL 5 (prototype 
methods validated in the target environment).  
Outcomes  
This project plan would progress development of an automated de -handing solution to TRL5. The 
methods described correspond to Automation Option 2 - Submersion De -hander, in the Feasibility 
Report for Improving Banana De -handing with Automation . This would test and/or deliver the 
following outcomes:  
o Validation of the banana de -handing technique.  
o Identification and testing of the minimum required equipment and robot degrees of 
freedom (DOF) to complete the task.  
o Testing of the detailed engineering design in a simulated target environment 
(working conditions, sap/bleed, lighting)  
o Benchmarking of the technical specification against current manual handling (time, 
quality/defects).  
o Provision of a basis for a cost benefit analysis – i.e. to determine capital and 
operational expenditure associated with technology implementation.  
Methods  
Due to the high confidence in the possibility of solving the de -handing problem with computer vision 
systems and existing robotics and end effector technologies, these solutions can be incorporated 
into the project plan.  
For example, line detection algorithms are very common in computer vision, and when faced with a 
complicated scene like that presented by a banana crown, a solution can generally be found by 
acquiring sufficient volumes of training data. The project therefore would depend upon the 
participation of banana growers for data collection and validation.  Similarly, based on experience, 
the project plan assumes that robotic arm proposed for development purposes would offer 
sufficient flexibility to enable changes in the system design without requiring new hardware.  
Given these considerations, and ability to identify and deploy appropriately skilled personnel, a two -
year project delivery duration is anticipated. In this time, the computer vision algorithms can be 
trained, the end effectors built and validated, and the  robotic systems integrated with associated 
hardware and software.

and end effectors.

Costings  
 
The provided costings (refer table 2) detail the estimated cost to progress automation option 2 to 
TRL 5, pending a detailed design phase and articulation of agreed technical specification. The cost 
outlined do not reflect a deployable system. For example,  the development cell requires a robot that 
can test through a range of degrees of freedom in order to determine the optimal degrees of 
freedom for the ultimate robotic solution and associated specifications. This process would produce 
a beta prototype tes ted in a representative environment and include the following components:  
1. Robot arm : Identify, purchase and commission a robot arm for handling banana bunches. 
We propose the use of an existing robot arm with capacity to manipulate a bunch of 
bananas. To enable infield testing, the robot used should have the appropriate IP (Ingress 
Prote ction) rating and effectively work in wet conditions.  
2. Robot arm path planning: Develop collision avoidance for the prototype robotic cell.  3. Secondary arm for cutting : Identify and purchase a secondary arm. The secondary arm 
needs to provide sufficient dexterity to cut banana hands while having an appropriate IP 
rating.  
4. Computer vision system: Identify and purchase a computer vision and sensor package for 
detecting banana hands and propose locations for cutting.  
5. Conveyor Development:  Identify and purchase components for a conveyer to lift bananas 
from the tank proposed in automation option 2 onto the wheel/through for processing.  
6. Interface with existing conveyor and overhead rail:  Develop algorithms and control to 
interface with the proposed conveyor and existing overhead banana rails.  
7. End-effector and cutting tool: Identify and purchase the appropriate cutting device from the 
proposals.

Identified Issues and Risks  
The primary risks to the delivery of a prototype banana de -handing system will concern the return 
on investment of the technology. The ARM Hub is confident that the chosen technologies (robotic 
arms, computer vision, etc.) are capable of performing the tas k at hand given enough development 
time, but these systems are sensitive to environmental issues that will be difficult to simulate in a 
laboratory environment where development is most cost -efficient.  
For example, computer vision systems are often sensitive to lighting conditions, and workspaces like 
a banana de -handing station are often exposed to the outdoor light and heavy shadowing. This can 
be overcome given enough simulation time and training data , but there is a risk that the simulated 
lighting conditions do not fully cover the range of conditions experienced on the farm. Incorporating 
more data and simulation time will incur additional costs, which may not be palatable to funders.  
In a similar vein, the amount of time it takes to develop a robotic cutting system that minimises the 
amount of sap and waste generated is expected take much longer than one that just successfully de -
hands bananas. It is anticipated that the problems/challenges can be solved given enough time but 
aren’t certain to be solved in an economical timeframe.  
Other risks to the project concern access both to data from farms and suitable project staff. Staffing 
is currently tight across the robotics industry and allocating researcher time for data collection may 
be an expensive component of the project. In the e vent that no staff are available for data collection 
or project work, the project would inevitably be delayed.

Removal of tree roots from pipes . 
Solutions for removal  
- High pressure water jet cutter  
o Pressure of around 5000 psi is used. The high -pressure water breaks up the tree 
roots and forces them through the pipe. This will remove all obstructions.  
- Robotic cutter  
o A robotic cutter is a specialized drainpipe tool with a diamond impregnated steel 
cutting head that can cut through obstructions with ease. The robotic cutting head is 
attached to an air hose that is inserted inside the pipe where it spins around and 
grind s away the obstruction. It can cut in a 360 degree motion which allows joints to 
be resurfaced effortlessly providing a smooth finish.  
Solutions for prevention  
- Chemical to flush roots to prevent – part time solution  
o Vapor rooter – Vapor  rooter Stops Tree Root Blockages in Pipes and Drains and 
Prevents Further Tree Root Damage  
o Root ox - A product which can be purchased from hardware and plumbing stores to 
remove and control tree roots within sewer pipes.  
Microwaves to remove tree roots  
- Research presents weeds can be killed using microwaves. A Professor from the University of 
Melbourne presents a case study that the weeds cells absorb the microwave radiation, 
breaking down the cell walls and killing the plant. Does this affect translate to tree roots?  
Microwaves can kill roots and plants,  but they can’t remove them from the pipe. Therefore, 
microwaves could offer a preventive solution to using chemicals that could be environmentally 
harmful. But the microwaves would only kill and not remove the roots.  
 
Notes :  
Sewer pipes are 150mm  in diameter in the street. Where the maximum sized pipe in the street is 
225mm , this pipes are often storm water pipes.

Key business objectives, priorities and timeframes  
Leakster outlined business go als, including:  
- A model (above ground) system that could be used to develop benchmark data  - Make  current  working prototype more industrialised to sell  – unique selling proposition is 
that this “unit” would enable smarter deployment of leak detection services rather current 
systems which require deployment across whole network.  
- Design for scaled up manufacture  
- Improved design and specifications to allow for better range (from 250m to 1 kilometre) and 
insights  (categories of leaks to improve prediction for repair costs) .  
- Ultimately, seek to develop the product/service b eyond leak detection to condition 
monitoring, including digital twin aspirations in long term.  
- Seeking to get rid of need for pipe inspection  – through v isualisation of the network.  
In the next development cycle, Leakster  seek s to progress to the deliver y of a suburb -scale 
demonstrator of both hardware and a software -as-a-service system  for leak detection in  utility managed 
water infrastructure.  
Leakster is currently contracted by  Urban Utilities to deliver a prototype solution for leak detection over 
1,000 kilometers of pipe.  The intention is that , once delivered, Leakster  will be well placed to further 
commercialise the delivery of their system /service , including  for other utilities . Sunshine Coast’s Unity 
Water has expressed interest. Have investors for seed raising if needed.  
The demonstrator would present  an in-ground (or in water meter) box deployed minimum viable 
product that utilis es and incorporates some further develop ment of  current hardware  and iOT 
functionalities . The system would be design ed for continuous monitoring with optimal  battery life  as 
well as for scaled manufacture and allow for further iterative hardware development.   
Product development and demonstration will deliver a model system for data capture and 
categorization – captur ing and labelling  of training data as basis for AI required to scale deployment.  
 
Background:  
Current industry standard is the use of l istening sticks – across pipeline to manually listen for leak s. Data 
is correlated between two points (or hydrants) in a pipe. Urban Utilities (UU) for example, manages 
8,000 kilometers of pipeline. Trace is undertaken once every 3 years. Current occurrence of leaks in UU 
pipes is  one every 3km. These are caused by a range of factors including ground movement from 
temperature changes.  
The solution/system is intended to deliver improved water conservation and asset management 
outcomes for Utilities.  
Leakster  indicated that trials and early tests have demonstrated that they can potentially deliver a 
software -as-service solution with their technology that will provide a more cost -effective solution with 
improved conservation and asset management outcomes than o thers in the market. Details of 
market/competitor analysis  
  Challenge or problem definition

Currently use listening sticks and manual tracing  
Cover the entire network every three years, which isn’t fast enough  
Raised a lot of capital and now have a working prototype  
Idea was to generate different sounds through the pipe and use TDR (time domain reflectometer) to 
analyse them  
Problem is a lack of accurate ground truth from the utility, so can’t use a learning model  
POC exists a t c. TRL 5

3. Need to determine system power source (battery/turbine)

and shows where the leak is.

where get best data.

background  to identify transients and then can send signals to track them.

moment . In metal pipe, consider should be able to get to 1km.

• System uses r aspberry pi, modem low noise studio audio basis, needs preamp for nighttime to 
bring the noise floor 3dB down when pipe is quieter.  
• Have sensor and receiver. Listeners (hydrophones in water); signal. Data for dispersion 
characteristics is unclear.  
• Within scope hardware may change . However, this would provide useful well spring of data for
